DAUGHTERS OF SAINT ANNE

PERPETUAL ADORATION CONTEMPLATIVES

THIRD READING OF THE LITURGY OF THE HOURS

Calendar of the Third Reading of the Divine Office

Sanctuary of Saint Anne — Diocese of Trapani

PRESENTATION

For each day, in the celebration of the Liturgy of the Hours, a text is indicated to be proclaimed after the second reading of the Office of Readings or at another liturgical Hour of the same day.

In choosing the contents, the principles and norms of the Liturgy of the Hours itself have been followed.

In fact, the cycle of biblical readings in the Office of Readings takes into account both the sacred seasons in which certain books are to be read and the cycle of readings at Mass.

Therefore, just as the Liturgy of the Hours is arranged so that the reading of Scripture in the Divine Office completes that of the Mass and provides a compendium of the whole history of salvation, in the same way the charismatic texts proposed here bring out the intimate link between salvation history and the charismatic mission of Mother Rosa and of her spiritual Family, placed by God under the spiritual guidance of Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate.

May Saint Anne, the Most Holy Virgin Mary, and Mother Rosa obtain for us a deep sharing in the work of human redemption and of the perfect glorification of God, which Christ accomplishes in the Holy Spirit through his Church, not only when she celebrates the Eucharist and the sacraments are administered, but also when the Liturgy of the Hours is celebrated (cf. SC no. 83).

Advent Season — Christmas Season

First Sunday of Advent

Tr. pp. 43-44, “Most Holy Mary… a new humanity”

The Most Holy Mary not only stands out among the humble, the poor, and the Saints who await the Lord, but, associated with Christ her Son, she gives full meaning to the promises: the redemption and the coming of the Messiah, who takes upon himself the sin of humanity: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike at your head, while you strike at his heel” (Gen 3:15). Here she is foreshadowed in the symbolic figure of the Daughter of Zion, which designates the people of God in what it has and preserves that is purest and most genuine. The Prophets greeted her in advance with psalms of joy and sorrow, pointing to the visitation of the Lord, the fulfillment of the promises, the redemption, the imminent coming of the Messiah, who takes the sin of humanity upon himself and associates her with himself in the liberating and creative mission of a new humanity.

Monday

Tr. pp. 49-51, par. 2.4 or Constitutions art. 6

The divine-human person of Christ Jesus will one day return in glory to judge humanity. For this reason all humanity looks to him and awaits him with confidence, for an eternal life, almost a deification of man, who has become, in the most marvelous way, a sharer and partaker in the infinite, eternal, most blessed life of God, an anticipation and assurance for all who live in this hope.

It does not seem out of place, therefore, to recall here the expectation and hope of the ancient Covenant. In its prophetic whole, a foreshadowing of the new Covenant, marked by the loftiest desire for the joyful expectation of the encounter with Jesus in glory, the ancient interior cry of prayer, “Come, Lord Jesus!”, takes on new vigor, meaning, consistency, and momentum. And it is a foretaste of Paradise. “Come, Lord Jesus!” not only in human form, but in the splendor of glory. Ultimately, Jesus is the first and the last word. The first, implicit in the Promise; the last, explicit, that of the last of the sacred Books: the Apocalypse. Every soul awaits him, even if it lives amid the appearances of a passing world, even if it seeks him where he is not, even when it rejects him because it does not know him.

With inspired and brilliant intuition, Mother Rosa raised the banner of hope as her program and her charism.

The hope poured out in us by the Spirit, sent by Jesus to all his followers, awakens in us the unquenchable desire to see God face to face. The Holy Spirit instills in us, with inexpressible groanings, a living and growing expectation of seeing God. What the Psalm says is thus fulfilled: “My soul thirsts for the living God: when shall I come and behold the face of God?”

And what does the soul seek, then, if not to see Your Face? This is the unanimous sigh of the ancient and the new Covenant. Mother Rosa mystically contemplated the face of the Father many times. With this light in her soul, the face of the Father becomes present in the face of the Crucified, beloved, guide, well-beloved, Eucharist, divine face visibly appeared in Jesus, the beloved Word.

To seek the face of God! In this connatural sigh of the soul, image of God, the spirituality of the ancient and of the new Covenant are wonderfully joined.

Tuesday

Tr. pp. 36-39, par. 1.2 or Constitutions art. 48

God, who reveals himself repeatedly in the history of Israel as One and Only, Holy and Eternal Living One, near, present, and active in the community of the chosen people, who reveals himself to individual persons such as the Patriarchs, Moses, and the Prophets, creates in the soul of those who listen to him and remain faithful to him the expectation of the fulfillment of the divine promise: the joyful event of the incarnate Word, the promised God-with-us (Isa 7:14). This expectation lasts centuries upon centuries and, with time, becomes more alive, more holily piercing, as can be well noted in the blessing words of the holy old man Simeon when he has the good fortune to receive Jesus in his arms, by now weary and weakened by incessant, suffering prayer, the fruit of a long waiting: “Now, Lord, let your servant go in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for the nations and the glory of your people” (Luke 2:29-32). Yes, the deep and universal prayer that bursts forth from the depths of the hearts of the covenant people can be summed up in two words: “Come, Lord Jesus!”

It is the prayer proper and characteristic of hope, the virtue that contains and qualifies the spirituality of Israel. The resounding miracle of the crossing of the Red Sea and the extraordinary wonders worked by God to free his people from slavery in Egypt prophetically magnified the hope of another passage still more marvelous, the astonishment of heaven and earth: the expectation of the man who would also be God. Thus the true passage took shape: from the slavery of guilt and its consequences to the entrance into the promised land of divinization in Christ; from a mortal life, subject to the miseries and unhappiness of sin, to the eternal and immortal life of grace, through the more than wondrous insertion of limited and troubled human life into the divine and eternal life by virtue of grace!

The suffered spiritual wisdom of detachment from the world (from the treacherous earth that holds the soul prisoner with its fascinating and vain enticements of the promised land of salvation) is truly a passage from extreme poverty, not only of material goods but above all the poverty of weakness and fragility of spiritual life, to the infinite riches of life in Christ.

The material poverty to which the covenant people is subject is a prophecy and a reminder of the nothingness of the creature and the all of God and of his grace (Ps 25:9; 9:19). In this sense, poverty contains the sum of all virtues, beginning with humility, the living sense of one’s own nothingness, of one’s native insufficiencies made worse by original sin, and of one’s own fragility before the mercy and the infinite, generous richness of God’s goodness, who sets no limits to his gifts, in order to restore to the human person the richness granted at the act of creation. These gifts, wonderfully increased, are guaranteed and made accessible by the grace of the head of the mystical body: Jesus Christ.

It is easy to understand, then, how this long waiting for the Messiah was felt more acutely by those poor in material goods, tried by poverty and by the misfortunes of slavery, of exile, of the loss of homeland, of loved ones, and of all well-being.

These experiences gave rise to the small and poor “remnant of Israel,” which thus learned to live in fidelity to the demands of Revelation, awaiting the fulfillment of the Lord’s promises. These were precisely the conditions willed by the God of the Covenant so that the goodness of the redeeming God might shine more clearly, even to surpassing the goodness of God the creator.

Wishing now to sum up in two words the explicit and implicit, outward and inward prayer of the people of the Covenant, marked by hope, enlivened by faith and by grateful love for God, we can certainly identify it with the sigh of every soul that lives in the atmosphere of the covenant: “Come to save the people, come, O Redeemer God! Tear through the shadow of waiting, come to free them from the slavery of guilt, come, O almighty and merciful God!”

Wednesday

Tr. pp. 76-78, “In every person the coming of the Kingdom is fulfilled… the passion and death of Jesus”

In every person the coming of the Kingdom is fulfilled to the extent that the person loves Christ, because the Kingdom is Jesus Christ himself, and his coming in glory is fulfilled to the extent that the believing person who loves God is filled with Jesus and identified with him.

Here lies the substance of the Christian spiritual life. Here lies the key to progress and growth in holiness: the universal vocation of those who choose Jesus Christ, Son of God, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

“Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:23). Among all the theological virtues, charity is the one that puts us in direct contact with God. “Charity, in a certain way, unlike every other virtue, unites directly to God” (Saint Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, III, Dist. 3, q. 1). “All the goodness of his soul is in charity” (S.Th. I Sent. Dist. 17, q. 9, B). “Charity is the life of the soul; as the soul is mutually and immediately united to the body, so charity immediately unites to God” (S.Th. II-II, q. 23). “The charity with which we love our neighbor is a participation in divine charity” (Ibid. a. 2 ad 2).

“The virtue of charity with which one loves God, oneself (not selfishly), and one’s neighbor is the same, just as the virtue of hope, with which one hopes for oneself and for others, is the same” (S.Th. II-II, q. 17, a. 3). “It can therefore be said that the love of God is hope in action, hope at work. The virtue of charity (of the love of God) is the gift in which all the other gifts are given to the soul” (S.Th. III Dist. 34, q. 1, a. 1). “Charity is the principle of all the other virtues, just as prudence is the principle that unites and regulates all the moral virtues” (III Dist. 27, q. 2, a. 4). Right and ordered love is included in every other virtue” (II-II, q. 125, a. 4). We can well understand, then, Jesus’ invitation: “Remain in my love and you will have every good” (John 15:9).

Hope grows strong and becomes great and deep on the foundation of faith, charity, and the love of God, because it is not reduced to the fragile thread of history! The ancient and new Covenant is something far greater than history itself. The incarnation of the Word, the first and indispensable foundation of the history of the Old and New Testaments, is the most astounding of God’s works. All the saved have had, and now have, salvation thanks to the merits of Christ, of infinite and ever-present value, under the movement of the Holy Spirit, both before the incarnation and after it, thanks to the passion and death of Jesus.

Thursday

Tr. p. 54 par. 3.1

The hope that the people chosen by God lived in the Old Testament, in the covenant pact made by God with the Patriarchs, with Moses and the Prophets, was founded on the word of God. Hope, the banner of Mother Rosa’s spirituality, is founded on the living and unshakable rock that is Jesus Christ himself.

The people of the new covenant, the Church born of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, walks in hope, awaiting the final glorious manifestation of Christ.

The presence between heaven and earth of an eternal high priest, who is the incarnate Word, cannot fail to have an effect on human beings. Humanity, reconformed to its Head through redemptive suffering and reconsecrated to the Father by the glory of the Son of Man, constitutes the Church, which is certainly the people of God, but also the new Eve born from the side of the new Adam, asleep on the cross in the sleep of a death that conquers death forever.

Friday

D. pp. 151-152, “In Saint Anne there is the dawn… and Savior of the world”

In Saint Anne there is the dawn of the day when: “…the nations shall behold your vindication, and all the kings your glory; you shall be called by a new name pronounced by the mouth of the Lord… No more shall people call you Forsaken, nor your land Desolate, but you shall be called My Delight, and your land Espoused, for the Lord delights in you and your land shall have a spouse…” (Isa 62:2, 4).

Anne is the daughter of Abraham and of David; she is a member of a people of the poor who with trust await and receive from him Salvation; she is the one who gives birth to the Handmaid of the Lord, and who awaits the Messiah-Servant, the Savior, the Redeemer, the Priest of the New and eternal Covenant.

God, therefore, manifests in the life of Anne his presence and his face as a merciful Father, Father of the humble and the poor. Father of the Poor Handmaid who “stands out among the humble,” Father of the Son-Servant, Crucified and Savior of the world.

Saturday

Tr. p. 80, “In the person of Jesus… all you his saints”

In the person of Jesus, then, the history of the ancient and new Covenant finds its origin and foundation. Their unity is constituted by Jesus who is to come, Jesus who has come, Jesus who comes. The ancient Covenant was a prelude and a prophecy of what would be revealed and accomplished in the new Covenant, personified in Jesus Christ, Son of the Father and Son of Mary, through his examples (Jesus teaches more by deeds than by words) and above all through the full adherence of his will to that of the Father at the supreme moment of accepting the passion and death. The ancient Covenant then turns into a song of love for God and neighbor, a love practiced and preached by Jesus Christ and already anticipated in many Psalms: “I love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps 18:2); “Love the Lord, all you his saints” (Ps 31:24).

Second Sunday of Advent

Tr. p. 34 “God in person… the Messiah to come”

God in person speaks to the Patriarchs, to Moses, to the Prophets, his spokesmen to the people. They will continue to proclaim the threats deserved by deviations and transgressions, the misfortunes that will not fail to come as a result of the people’s repeated infidelities to the covenant. At the first sign of repentance, however, these threats will be promptly repaired with an abundance of new graces and new favors. The history of the covenant people thus lives out a course woven of divine pedagogy, which reaches a high point before and after the slavery and the liberation from Egypt. This pedagogy prepares the covenant people for the supreme event of history: the Incarnation and the Redemption.

It is, therefore, the teaching of the spiritual life, imparted by God to his people through the word, the writings, and the practice of penance. He trains them to recognize him as the one and only God, to contemplate and give thanks for created things, to respect and love their neighbor, to detach themselves from what is their own, up to the supreme sacrifice of detachment from their homeland. With the homeland, God takes from the people everything they have, in order to give it back to them later in a new way and in greater measure. It is the salutary exercise of poverty, a prelude to the poverty of the Messiah to come.

Monday

D. pp. 156-157, par. 4

In the presence of Anne, as in the life of every saint, the divine action of the Father, his will and holiness, is manifested.

In the signs and interior words with which Saint Anne mystically transmits her message to Rosa, one finds a harmony with the signs and words she receives directly from the Father, from Christ, from the Spirit, and from Mary.

For her mission among the sick, we have seen how, bound up with the blessing of the oil for the sick, there is for Rosa the sending by the Father to care for the sick.

He confirms this same sending through the person of Saint Anne, who, on a March 1st of an uncertain year, places in Rosa’s hands a supernatural energy: that power of the Spirit that goes forth from Christ in the acts of healing and cure; “…power came forth from him and healed all” (Luke 6:19).

She notes down in a page of a notebook the event that concerns her:

“March 1st, from the Holy Mother Anne I received in my hands a light, in the center of the hands. And she said: ‘From now on all the sick whom you bless will be healed; always in the name of God you will bless them and they will be healed.’”

It is evident that the Father entrusts to Rosa with special love the care of the sick and thus makes her a sharer in the very mission of the Son, who “healed all.”

Of Jesus, the Gospel of Mark emphasizes: “He laid his hands on a few sick people and cured them”; “He laid his hands on him and asked, ‘Do you see anything?’” (Mark 6:5; 8:23). To the apostles also Jesus entrusts with priority the mission of preaching so that people may be converted, of freeing from demons, and of healing the sick (cf. Mark 6:12-13).

Tuesday

Tr. pp. 150-151 “The Church… clothed in glory”

The Church, that is, the kingdom of Christ already present in mystery by the power of God, grows visibly in the world. This beginning and this growth are signified by the blood and water that flowed from the open side of the crucified Christ and are foretold by the Lord’s words about his death on the cross: “And when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw everyone to myself” (John 12:32). Every time the sacrifice of the cross, “by which Christ our Paschal Lamb has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7), is celebrated on the altar, the work of our redemption is renewed. And together with the sacrament of the Eucharistic bread, the unity of the faithful, who form one body in Christ, the light of the world, is represented and brought about; from him we come, through him we live, toward him we are headed” (LG 3).

In this truly wonderful sense, Jesus is our hope and the Church is truly the Ark of the Covenant, prefigured in the ancient Covenant, divinely realized in the new and eternal Covenant.

The Church is therefore the beginning on earth of the kingdom of Christ and of God.

In the light of this splendid theology of the Church, the various images of the Church outlined by the Council are brilliantly understood: “the Church is the sheepfold whose one and necessary door is Christ; it is the flock of which Christ himself is the Good Shepherd and chief of shepherds; it is God’s field in which grows the ancient olive tree whose holy root was the patriarchs…; the Church is God’s building, of which the Lord is the cornerstone, the foundation on which the Church itself is built and from which it will receive stability and cohesion. The Church is the house where his family dwells, the dwelling of God with men; it is the new Jerusalem, the Holy City. In it, as living stones, we form a spiritual temple. This holy city Saint John, in the Apocalypse, contemplates in its final phase, coming down from God as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:1ff.).

The Church is the heavenly Jerusalem, “our mother,” the immaculate bride of the immaculate Lamb.

And while the Church fulfills her pilgrimage on this earth far from the Lord (cf. 2 Cor 5:6), she is like an exile who seeks and desires the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, until with her Bridegroom she appears clothed in glory (cf. Col 3:1-4)” (cf. LG 6, 7).

Wednesday

Tr. pp. 40-41 “To Saint Anne… walk before me and be perfect”

To Saint Anne we can therefore attribute the traits of the authentic “poor one of God,” in the deepest sense of the word, that is, a person who is humble, simple, devout, poor, yet rich in goodness, in charity, in a piety such that she sums up in herself the aspirations of Israel, of the history and mission of the entire people of the Covenant, becoming an instrument for the fulfillment of the messianic promises, a firm bond of union and continuity between the ancient and the new Covenant, a sign of the goodness of God the Father, the infinite and primary source of all fatherhood and all motherhood.

Without doubt Saint Anne spent her days in humility, in poverty, in daily work, and above all in prayer centered on the fulfillment of the expected Promises, and in charity toward her neighbor.

How could the holy mother of the Immaculate One have practiced all this rich heritage of virtues — poverty, humility, charity, piety — had she not continually lived in all its fullness the principle that God himself placed at the foundation of all the spirituality of messianic expectation, a principle that grounds and sustains, as a cornerstone, every other virtue? It is, in practice, the principle revealed by God himself to Abraham at the very moment he was making the Covenant with him, as if offering “the Father of our faith” a means of the highest value for remaining faithful to the Pact: “Walk before me and be perfect” (Gen 17:1).

Thursday

Tr. p. 155 “After the long waiting… a man who is God”

After the long waiting for the promise, we see the Covenant concentrated in the family of Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate One, and in a particular way in the person of Mary, who marks the dawn of Redemption.

The personalization of the Covenant thus reaches the extreme limit of the creature in the Most Holy Mary, whose birth is an announcement of joy for the whole universe.

The Most Holy Mary is the mother of the new Covenant by the very fact that she is Mother of the eternal Word, of God-with-us. Thus is realized the indissoluble Covenant of the divine nature with the human nature in Jesus Christ, a divine person, in whom the Covenant coincides with the mystery of the incarnation. Two natures, the divine and the human, become one person: the divine person of the Word.

God sealed the Covenant in a truly divine way: a God who becomes Man; a man who is God!

Friday

Tr. pp. 46-47 par. 2.1

The wonder of the holiness of the Most Holy Mary, of the glory she gives to God, of the delight that through her is poured out on all humanity, takes on consistency and value because Mary is intimately associated with the mediating and redeeming work of Christ, in whom the new Covenant is realized, a relationship not only between God and man, but an indissoluble bond that unites the two natures in the one person of Christ.

Humanity is assumed into the divine nature of the eternal Word of God. In the divine Redeemer, the fullness of divinity and the fullness of humanity are fused together, realizing in an immensely stronger way the Covenant of God with humanity, a relationship of mutual friendship between God and the people of Israel.

The Son of God, assuming human nature, while remaining God and being from eternity one nature with the Father, without confusion and without separation, truly becomes Man. The two natures constitute one divine Person. Here is the new Covenant, which is the incarnation of the Word, Jesus Christ himself. Christ became “poor” in a divinely profound sense. The idea of “poverty” cannot therefore be limited to simple poverty of an economic kind, because in that way Jesus would simply be an exemplary model to imitate, while the true mystery of Christ, which is the redeeming incarnation, would be left out. The poverty of Christ certainly also refers to material poverty: he is born in a poor cave, has a poor manger as his bed, is wrapped in poor swaddling clothes by his most holy Mother… aspects that allow us to give exceptional emphasis to his willed material poverty, but, as already said, it is of a divinely profound order.

Saturday

Tr. pp. 51-52 par. 2.5

Closely and indissolubly associated with the work of redemption, “as a generous companion and altogether exceptional collaborator of her Son the Redeemer” (cf. LG 61), the Most Holy Mary, the humble handmaid of the Lord, totally offered to the person and work of Christ, is under him and with him at the service of the mystery of redemption, becoming a cause of salvation.

What a marvelous opening to hope is the mother of God and our mother for us!

God willed to reach us through the powerful mediation and the maternal help of Mary.

Mother Rosa has a clear grasp of this precise identity and of Mary’s exalted mission in God’s plan of salvation. For this reason, by calling the members of her spiritual Family “Daughters” [and Sons] of Saint Anne, she does nothing other than place at the center the maternal function of the Most Holy Mary, inasmuch as the presence of Saint Anne clearly points to the wondrous power and greatness of her Daughter, Immaculate and most holy, proclaimed our mother by Jesus on Calvary, constituted forever mediatrix to the Mediator (cf. The Gift of God…, pp. 137-138; 142-143), Mother par excellence of all humanity.

In this sense one can well understand why God willed that all graces should come to us through the hands of Mary.

Third Sunday of Advent

Tr. pp. 87-88, “Identification with Christ… being drawn to what is lowly”

Identification with Christ the Poor One, the true fulcrum of the Institute’s spirituality, finds its characteristic expression in humility, which is the hinge of the life and teaching of Jesus: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt 11:29). This will be all the more broadly and deeply true if the expression “poor Jesus” is understood in the wide and strong sense in which Saint Paul says it: “For you know the gracious act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Cor 8:9). The Letter to the Philippians states the meaning of Jesus’ poverty even more strongly: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God something to be grasped. Rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, coming in human likeness; and found human in appearance, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross. Because of this, God greatly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Phil 2:6-11).

In the light of Jesus, the daughters of Saint Anne and those who are called by Christ to imitate this particular attitude of his, choosing the last places, serving, as he himself did, with all gentleness and kindness, and working tirelessly for the extension of the Kingdom, aware that the gifts received are for the common good, must make their own the words of the Gospel: “When you have done all that you have been commanded, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10), not aspiring to greatness but letting themselves be drawn to what is lowly (cf. Rom 12:16).

Monday

Tr. pp. 110-111, “Delaying for centuries the fulfillment… of Mary his daughter”

By delaying for centuries the fulfillment of the promise contained in the pact, God nevertheless lets us almost touch with our hands the abyss of misery into which sin had cast man, turning the earthly paradise into a valley of tears (Gen 3:14-19), beginning already with the killing of Abel by his brother Cain (cf. Gen 4:8), a crime that then spread into the fratricidal wars proper to the history of Israel, aggravated by an unbroken series of sufferings, defeats, slavery, and violence. It is precisely this succession of evils that renews the hope of the Savior.

The hope of Israel thus becomes a profound desire full of anguish, all the more keenly felt the more certain was the faith in the fulfillment of the promises by the One who does not deceive and cannot deceive and, above all, never fails to show effectively his goodness and mercy.

And yet how many times the ancient Covenant entered into crisis, not on God’s part but on the part of his people. It is enough to recall the events of the return from Egypt to the promised land: the repeated complaints against Moses were in fact complaints against God, who had chosen Moses as a strong and faithful leader and guide. And yet how many times Moses had to appease God’s wrath over the infidelities of his people, who even went so far as to replace him with an idol, the golden calf, made by Aaron and celebrated as their true God. And this after so many proofs of wondrous and fatherly assistance.

Infidelity to the Covenant was repeated, in any case, many times in the history of the chosen people. Great Prophets were then sent by God to remind the people of the divine promises, prophets almost always mistreated and even put to death.

All this shows the fragility of a Covenant that rests, on the one hand, on human beings and, on the other, on the word of God. And to the extent that the Covenant enters into crisis, hope enters into crisis. God, however, never fails his word. And when the people abandon him, he comes to meet them with the wonders of his mercy.

In this way we understand how the whole history of Israel is the living history of God’s mercy toward his people, because his mercy is infinite, as the Psalms say. This mercy renews hope time after time, concentrated and revived in the saints and above all in the splendid holiness of the mother of the Immaculate One and of Mary, her daughter.

Tuesday

Tr. pp. 111-112 “God willed to give hope… almost divinizing him”

God willed to give hope a foundation of absolute firmness in the new Covenant through an indissoluble union between himself and man in the mystery of the incarnation, a Covenant superior to every possible crisis; indeed, a Covenant that would never again enter into crisis, because it is realized in Jesus Christ, a union of absolute security between God and humanity, remaining forever truly God and truly man.

It is a matter of accepting in faith this marvelous encounter of the Word with humanity. Here lies the basis of hope, which will unite in Jesus Christ the fullness of human nature and the fullness of divine nature. On this basis hope can no longer suffer crises or infidelities, which are overcome in Christ, who is able to heal promptly and divinely the infidelities of individuals and of the people: the mystical body of the Church.

The people of God, through the Church, is united to Christ, the incarnate Word, as his Bride, as his mystical body. Not even the forces of hell can crack this divine covenant, which thus acquires a stability as strong as the omnipotence of God. Here is the new and divinely stable commandment of hope in the New Testament.

Nevertheless, the freedom of the individual is not taken away. The individual may not accept it, but can no longer break it, even though he may deny it and be lost.

To bring man back within the Covenant, Jesus instituted the sacrament of Mercy, for anyone who repents and is fully readmitted into intimacy with God, and the sacrament of the Eucharist, which identifies and transforms him to the point of making him one with himself, almost divinizing him.

Wednesday

Tr. pp. 131-132, par. 3.3

The daughters of Saint Anne and all who belong to the Family of the Mother of the Immaculate One are called to be a prophetic sign of the merciful love of the Father, of the unconditional offering of Christ Jesus, of hope, the fruit of the Spirit.

By their very presence they seek to be credible witnesses for all people, so that they may open themselves to salvation and be able to share in the integral freedom brought by Christ. Therefore they comfort, help, and make their own the anxieties and concerns of those who suffer; they bring relief to the sick and the marginalized, awakening their hope in the Lord Jesus and in his promises, and help them discover the precious essence of suffering in the light of his passion.

In the suffering and the marginalized they moreover recognize and serve Christ Crucified, who considers done to himself whatever is done to the weakest, the most forgotten, and the poorest, and they confidently accompany the hopes of man, orienting them toward the path of the covenant that will be definitively fulfilled in the beatific vision, in the splendor of the glory of the Father contemplated forever.

To accomplish this they readily and watchfully follow the action of the Spirit, and work diligently to gather the whole human family around the Father, in the certainty that God alone and his Kingdom are absolute.

Thus, with the whole Church, in prayer and with the heart, they cry out day and night: Come, Lord Jesus!

Thursday

Tr. pp. 58-59, par. 3.4

Christ, the great prophet, who by the witness of his life and the power of his word proclaimed the kingdom of the Father, fulfills his prophetic office until the full manifestation of his glory (LG 35).

In him all the faithful, made sharers in his mystical body through the outpouring of his Holy Spirit, form a holy and royal priesthood, offer spiritual sacrifices to God through him, and proclaim the wonders of the one who called them out of darkness into his wonderful light. There is therefore no member in the Church who does not have a part in the mission of the whole body, but each of them must sanctify Jesus in his heart and bear witness to him in a spirit of prophecy (cf. PO 2), so that the power of the Gospel may shine forth. The Church is truly a prophetic, priestly, and royal people, not only through baptism, but also through the Eucharist, where Jesus exercises his eternal priesthood, which is at once sacrifice and sacrament. The sacrifice of the Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the cross.

In the Eucharist, Jesus, the eternal priest, continues to offer himself mystically, to exercise his priesthood, as head of the Church, his mystical body. Baptism, which makes the Christian holy because it confers sanctifying grace, lays the foundations of Christian perfection and makes the baptized a sharer in the priesthood of Jesus and in his prophetic power. The members of Mother Rosa’s charismatic Family, committed to living their baptism intensely, grow in the prophetic dimension, which reveals the saving and merciful love of God, and cooperate with all their strength in the expansion and growth of the Kingdom of Christ in the world, serving Christ in others and leading to him, with humility and patience, all their brothers and sisters (cf. LG 35; 36).

Friday

Tr. pp. 113-114 “The new covenant… and to perfect communion with him”

The new Covenant thus involves us to the point of being, with Jesus and in Jesus, one with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; it involves us not only as members of the mystical body and of the people of God that is the Church, but also personally. The Covenant of the New Testament is not only a covenant with a people, but a covenant of God with each individual person, because God knows us personally and each person is everything to God, as if he or she were the only reality created by him. It is not for nothing that he wanted to reach us with the maternal tenderness of a Mother.

Each of us before God is therefore an only son and an only daughter, and thus infinitely beloved.

In Christ Jesus we all share in his uniqueness and in the infinite benevolence of God the Father toward his Only-Begotten.

In Jesus we are loved by the Father as the Father loves the Son, who loved us to the point of death on the cross.

What a marvel the reality of the new Covenant holds, and to what richness of perfection Jesus has brought it! The greatness, the security, the indissolubility of the new helps us appreciate the old better. The wonderful bond of the redeeming Covenant becomes a grand motive and foundation of hope.

From this perspective Christian life and holiness rest on such firm hinges that they cannot fail to become a witness for those who accept and live them fully, to the point of proclaiming them by life, example, word, and action turned into charity toward God, brothers and sisters.

It is not possible to identify with Jesus through prayer and the sacraments, above all the Eucharist, without becoming one with him. And since Jesus is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the spiritual Family of Mother Rosa carries out the thought and example of Jesus by letting itself be guided by the Spirit on the journey that leads it to full adherence to the Father’s will and to perfect communion with him.
Beginning of the Christmas Novena

Day 17

Tr. pp. 39-40, “Saint Anne belongs… his glorious dwelling”

Saint Anne belongs to the people of the Covenant and particularly to the “small remnant,” a truth that can be deduced from God’s own promise:

“Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another… The Lord listened attentively and heard them… They shall be… my own on the day I take action… For lo, the day is coming, burning like an oven, when all the proud and all evildoers will be stubble… But for you who fear my name, there will arise the sun of justice with healing rays…” (Mal 3:16-20).

If she saw the sun of justice rise in her house, there is no doubt that Saint Anne lived with such inner impetus the waiting made of hope, faith, and full trust in the promises of the Most High that she merited the grace of being chosen as mother of the Immaculate One, dawn of Redemption, guarantee of the divine promises: “But a shoot shall sprout from the stump of Jesse, and from his roots a bud shall blossom. The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength, a spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord… On that day, the root of Jesse, set up as a signal for the nations… his dwelling shall be glorious” (Isa 11:1-2, 10ff.).

Day 18

Tr. p. 43, “Saint Anne, the mother of the Immaculate One… united to his divinity”

Saint Anne, the mother of the Immaculate One, can also sing with her daughter Mary the Magnificat of thanksgiving. She is the mother of the one who incomparably surpasses the holiness of all creatures of heaven and earth, angelic and human, of the one who is greeted by the Archangel, in the name of God the Father: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you!” Full of grace, yes! Full of grace as no other angelic or human creature! The Lord is with you as with no other creature. One cannot, in fact, conceive of a creature holier than Mary, who reaches the very boundaries of divinity, as the holy Fathers say. Such had to be the Mother of the Incarnate Word, of the humanity of Christ, personally united to his divinity.

Day 19

Tr. pp. 78-79, “It is a marvelous work… deepest meaning and its root”

The work of creation, especially of the human person, is a marvelous work, worthy of almighty God. Immeasurably greater is the work of redemption, so that the Church does not hesitate to declare: God was wonderful in the work of creating human nature, but more wonderful still is to have restored and renewed it through Jesus Christ.

The event of the two Covenants, ancient and new, must be placed in a metahistorical perspective, that is, one that is above history and is the foundation of history, which is the work of Redemption.

Creation, on which all history is founded, is itself a metahistorical intervention of God. It is God who freely and gratuitously expands ad extra (outside himself) the infinite fire of his love. The redeeming work therefore continues and extends in the most stupendous way, truly worthy of God, his love for creatures; or rather, for the masterpiece of creation, which is precisely man.

The whole history of the ancient and new Covenant is centered on the divine person of Jesus, Son of God and Son of man, that is, son of the Virgin Mary, the Immaculate One.

At the foundation of salvation history, therefore, lies God’s love for the human person.

Creation and redemption are thus realities that can be traced back to the love God has for the human creature, the first origin of all history, which finds in the incarnate Word its deepest meaning and its root.

Day 20

Tr. pp. 105-106, “As a chosen member… her mission”

As a chosen member of the “Remnant of Israel,” Mary nourishes her prayer with the Word of God and receives into her soul the message of the psalms, turning it into vital fabric that illumines her actions and opens her to the universal embrace of the saving action of her Savior.

Union with God, the specific vocation of her people, is accomplished in her to such a degree that she becomes, by divine and gratuitous grace, the Mother of the eternal Word: the Messiah awaited by Israel, the Redeemer who, by associating her with his redemptive plan, makes her Mother of Humanity.

Contemplating Mary, the members of the Family of the holy Mother live their commitment in the Church in prayer and poverty of heart, which for them is a way of being, living, and existing that characterizes their presence in the world and shapes their lifestyle, both familial and apostolic.

Contemplation, prayer, “poverty of heart, which Mother Rosa embodied in her own existence, driven by her ardent desire to identify herself with Christ, emptied even to death on a cross, with the One she used to call ‘my Good’ and whose very path she longed to travel, her gaze fixed on Mary as the perfect model of what she experienced as her most intimate vocation: ‘Useless slave of my Jesus, my beloved Paradise’” (Const., art. 6).

The emphasis on Mary’s presence has great and exceptional significance for the Daughters of Saint Anne and for the other followers of Mother Rosa, and helps us understand their spirit. In harmony with their very name, it designates them as sisters and brothers of the Most Holy Mary, formed in the same school and continuers of her mission.

Day 21

Tr. pp. 127-128, par. 2.4

Knowledge of the mystery of Christ is followed by love and devotion toward his mother.

Those who in every generation, among the various peoples and nations of the earth, receive with faith the mystery of Christ, the incarnate Word and Redeemer of the world, not only turn with veneration and have confident recourse to Mary as to his Mother, but seek in her faith support for their own faith (cf. RM 27).

If Mary, his Mother and ours, is present in our prayer with Jesus, it reaches the Father more pleasing and more effective for our personal salvation and for that of so many souls today so far from God.

In this spiritual horizon, the daughters of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family of the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, in awaiting the Lord who comes, attune their prayer to that of the Church, which from the beginning of her earthly journey contemplates the Mother of God and constantly repeats with her the words of the Magnificat. They contemplate her with special devotion as the daughter of Saint Anne and as her prolongation in salvation history. With the Church they love her, seeking to become like her; they maintain a bond that embraces the saving mystery she represents: past, present, future; and they venerate her as spiritual mother of humanity, mother of Grace and Mercy.

Day 22

Tr. pp. 104-105 “The daughters (sons)… divine blessing upon humanity”

The daughters [sons] of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family follow Christ, the poor one par excellence, and contemplate Mary, who not only stands out among the humble and poor of the Lord but incomparably transcends them, to the point of drawing God’s gaze: “He has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid.” Precisely because of this supreme poverty she was filled with the fullness of grace on earth and of glory in heaven and throughout the centuries of human history: “All generations will call me blessed.”

In the Magnificat, Mary reveals the praying soul that synthesizes in herself, in a mature way, the praise, blessing, prayer, supplication, offering, waiting, and gratitude of her ancestors, of all those, that is, who with their lives glorified God.

She draws reasons for contemplation and exultation from her own personal experience with God, in whom she perceives herself as a link in the long chain of human history.

Formed in the contemplation of the events and wonders of God handed down by Scripture, shaped early in the sense of a personal relationship with him, as an authentic “poor one,” her prayer becomes absolute openness and docility when the mysterious event of the Incarnation involves her personally.

Prayer forms her to grasp all the passages of God in her history and in that of humanity; therefore she proclaims him: my Savior, Almighty and Holy.

The contemplation of God detaches her from herself to such a point that she perceives herself in him as a “handmaid” who, by her humility and fullness, has drawn divine blessing upon humanity.

Day 23

Tr. pp. 147-148, par. 1.6

The supreme masterpiece of every masterpiece is the holiness of the Most Holy Mary, so docile to the Holy Spirit, to his graces, his gifts, his inspirations, that she becomes his collaborator in the work of the sanctification of souls.

The Most Holy Mary is not only a masterpiece to admire and contemplate, but a presence to prolong and a model to embody. She is the active collaborator of the Holy Spirit, the living, eloquent example and unsurpassable teacher of docility to his action, a most perfect imitator of the Son, most obedient to the will of the Father.

After Jesus, the way, the truth, and the life, in the work of our sanctification we look to the Most Holy Mary, Mother in the order of grace.

Mother Rosa’s experience: “Oh Mary, through you I am saved, through you I am a religious. The fire of your Son’s love, Mary, you kindled many times with your hands in this heart of your Son” (Memoirs 4.4, p. 56) reveals how much she trusted in Mary’s maternal intercession and how she contemplated her as the daughter of Saint Anne, the perfect model of docility to the Spirit, who made her the perfect image of Jesus her Son, the Poor One, in whom “the Father was well pleased.”

Day 24

D. pp. 137-138, par. 2

In some experiences of infused contemplation, Rosa sees the Mother with the Child beside the divine Father. A presence that leads us to consider the nature of the bond that joins them in the Economy of Salvation and that is an existential message for her:

“I saw my Eternal Father with a smiling face; he pointed out to me a vacant place; and then Mary with the Child, my Jesus, in her arms, in the act of handing him to me…” (M. 1.1, p. 39).

God’s Economy toward her shows a link between her life and that of Mary with the Child.

In the light of the History of Salvation, the Mother with the Child and the presence of the Eternal Father attest the reality of Mary in God, who from eternity thought of her and created her with the most exalted dignity of being Mother of the Son begotten, not created. For Rosa, therefore, in the perspective of the gift received, Mary is the Mother of Jesus, her Son and eternal Son of the Father; she is the Mother of God with her most exalted dignity in heaven and on earth, in her mission and function, in relation to creation and to the plan of the Incarnation and Redemption.

December 25, Nativity of the Lord

D. pp. 139-140, par. 4

Through a vision of Mary with the Child, Saint Joseph, and the shepherds of Bethlehem, she learns in an unforgettable way the value of poverty of spirit.

The details present there highlight the poor who are close to Jesus and allow us to glimpse her process of purification so as to be welcomed by him and by Mary:

“…I found myself at the crib, but it seemed to me that Jesus and Mary also… preferred the shepherds… I went to the feet of Saint Joseph and begged him to cover my wickedness and obtain for me from the Most Holy Virgin that I might remain at the feet of Jesus… All at once both the Mother and the Son changed… and they appeared so sweet to me…” (M. 11.2, pp. 11-12).

The symbolism of the seriousness of the faces of the Mother and the Son calls her to conversion, challenges her, makes her attentive to making room for those present, not to separate the faith and love she has for Jesus and Mary from love toward others.

She learns from the Mother and the Son the way of humility, of descent, of losing one’s life for others in order to find it again. She learns from the Mother, associated with the life of the Son, to become attentive, delicate, to give joy and room to the humble and the poor, following the indications of God’s lowering of himself, who takes delight in Mary’s absolute poverty and gratuitousness.

Rosa, after being purified, finds herself at Mary’s feet more humble, at peace, free, and enjoys the joy of the little ones. She thus enters with all of herself into the mystery of the birth of Jesus, the Poor One of the Father.

The event of Christmas, also reported by the Gospels, asserts itself with all truth, efficacy, and startling relevance in her life: it is the poor who recognize in the Mother with the Child the One and the One who had been promised by God to save the world, winning the victory over evil (Gen 3:15).

December 26

Tr. p. 49, par. 2.3

The poverty of Jesus is also full, absolute, total acceptance of and adherence to the will of the Father, so that he is not only the Mediator (here is the new personal Covenant between God and man) but the Redeemer who takes upon himself the sins of all men and, by his sorrowful passion, death, and resurrection, wins complete victory over sin, hell, and death. In this way he gives back to man in superabundant measure the divine life of grace, becoming, through luminous teachings and even more through his examples, the light of the world for all humanity (John 8:12).

Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word, is truly the new Covenant in the strong sense: God and man are in him one Person, the Mediator by essence between God and man, at once priest and victim, repairer of all the faults and failures of humanity. He is the first, inexhaustible source, the most solid rock of hope for all humanity, the liberator from the prince of this world (the devil), the guarantor of salvation and eternal life, and the principle of a hope immensely deeper than that of the Old Testament, a hope that will never fail because it is tied to him.

December 27

Tr. pp. 46-47, par. 2.1

The wonder of the holiness of the Most Holy Mary, of the glory she gives to God, of the delight that through her is poured out on all humanity, takes on consistency and value because Mary is intimately associated with the mediating and redeeming work of Christ, in whom the new Covenant is realized, a relationship not only between God and man, but an indissoluble bond that unites the two natures in the one person of Christ.

Humanity is assumed into the divine nature of the eternal Word of God. In the divine Redeemer, the fullness of divinity and the fullness of humanity are fused together, realizing in an immensely stronger way the Covenant of God with humanity, a relationship of mutual friendship between God and the people of Israel.

The Son of God, assuming human nature, while being God and being from eternity one nature with the Father, without confusion and without separation, truly becomes Man. The two natures constitute one divine Person. Here is the new Covenant, which is the incarnation of the Word, Jesus Christ himself. Christ became “poor” in a divinely profound sense. The idea of “poverty” cannot therefore be limited to simple poverty of an economic kind, because in that way Jesus would simply be an exemplary model to imitate, while the true mystery of Christ, which is the redeeming incarnation, would be left out. The poverty of Christ certainly also refers to material poverty: he is born in a poor cave, has a poor manger as his bed, is wrapped in poor swaddling clothes by his most holy Mother… aspects that allow us to give exceptional emphasis to his willed material poverty, but, as already said, it is of a divinely profound order.

December 28

Tr. pp. 138-139, “Charity as the bond… fruitfulness in the world”

Charity, as the bond of perfection and fulfillment of the law (cf. Col 3:14; Rom 13:10), governs all the means of sanctification, gives them form, and leads them to their fulfillment. Therefore the true disciple of Christ is marked by charity both toward God and toward neighbor, Jesus Christ having shown his charity by laying down his life for us: no one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends (cf. John 15:13).

Christians are called to bear witness to the love, the charity, the gift they have received before men and especially before those who persecute them, even to the point of risking their own lives. Martyrdom, if necessary, makes them like the Master who freely accepts death for the salvation of the world. And as Lumen Gentium 42 teaches, “All must be prepared to confess Christ before men and to follow him along the way of the cross, through the persecutions which the Church never lacks.”

Other means the Lord offers to promote the holiness of the Church are the counsels he proposes to his disciples (cf. Matt 19:11; 1 Cor 7:7), so that more easily, with an undivided heart (cf. 1 Cor 7:32-34), they may consecrate themselves to God alone in virginity and celibacy. This perfect continence for the sake of the kingdom of heaven has always been held in singular honor by the Church, as a sign and stimulus of charity and a special source of spiritual fruitfulness in the world.

December 29

Tr. pp. 36-37, “God who reveals himself… by virtue of grace!”

God, who reveals himself repeatedly in the history of Israel as One and Only, Holy and Eternal Living One, near, present, and active in the community of the chosen people, who reveals himself to individual persons such as the Patriarchs, Moses, and the Prophets, creates in the soul of those who listen to him and remain faithful to him the expectation of the fulfillment of the divine promise: the joyful event of the incarnate Word, the promised God-with-us (Isa 7:14). This expectation lasts centuries upon centuries and, with time, becomes more alive, more holily piercing, as can be well noted in the blessing words of the holy old man Simeon when he has the strength to receive Jesus in his arms, by now weary and weakened by incessant, suffering prayer, the fruit of a long waiting: “Now, Lord, let your servant go in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for the nations and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:29-32). Yes, the deep and universal prayer that bursts forth from the depths of the hearts of the covenant people can be summed up in two words: “Come, Lord Jesus!”

It is the prayer proper and characteristic of hope, the virtue that contains and qualifies the spirituality of Israel. The resounding miracle of the crossing of the Red Sea and the extraordinary wonders worked by God to free his people from slavery in Egypt prophetically magnified the hope of another passage still more marvelous, the astonishment of heaven and earth: the expectation of the man who would also be God. Thus the true passage took shape: from the slavery of guilt and its consequences to the entrance into the promised land of divinization in Christ; from a mortal life, subject to the miseries and unhappiness of sin, to the eternal and immortal life of grace, through the more than wondrous insertion of limited and troubled human life into the divine and eternal life by virtue of grace!

December 30

FS p. 206, “The following of Christ… hiddenness and obedience”

Following Christ demands readiness and courage; one must answer the Master’s invitation as Peter and the other apostles did; he is not satisfied with mediocrity but wants generous hearts: this is how Mother Rosa spurs on her daughters (Letter to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: 2/12/1867; to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 4/23/1867).

Jesus is the model, the mirror in which a daughter of St. Anne must look at herself, learning from him to find true joy in adversity and to practice the evangelical virtues. One must “make good use of the lessons of such a teacher and be diligent in order to please him and fully satisfy his will” (Letter to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 2/4/1871).

She invites them to go to the school of Bethlehem, where the “God made little” offers us splendid lessons in detachment, self-emptying, and poverty. She likewise recommends attending the school of Nazareth, which speaks of hiddenness and obedience.

December 31

Tr. pp. 66-67, “Faith makes us believe… but increase our faith”

Faith makes us believe firmly in the word of God, of which Abraham (Gen 15:6) gave heroic proof, ready for the gravest of sacrifices, fully abandoned to the infinite merciful goodness of God.

No less is Moses’ full, trusting abandonment to God on so many occasions during the long, troubled pilgrimage toward the promised land. His faith is such that it turns into full confidence and trust, to the point of staying God’s threats, justly angered by the people’s many infidelities. This faith, resting entirely on the promise of the future Redeemer, is the prelude to Christian faith, not only in Jesus Christ as Messiah, but essentially as God, identical with the Father under the veils of human flesh, as today under the veils of bread and wine.

The key point of Christian faith is therefore to believe in the divinity of Christ, proclaimed by John in the Prologue of his Gospel and explicitly confirmed by Jesus himself more than once: “Before Abraham came to be, I AM” (John 8:58).

The clear testimony of his divinity will in fact be the decisive reason for his condemnation to death by crucifixion. To the high priest who asks him, “I order you to tell us under oath before the living God whether you are the Son of God,” Jesus answers: “You have said so.” Then Caiaphas tears his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed! What further need have we of witnesses?” And the Sanhedrin decrees: “He deserves to die” (Matt 26:62ff.). Jesus openly testifies to his divinity. In the face of this testimony the sentence of death follows immediately: “He has claimed to be the Son of God. We have no need of witnesses.” Those present were all witnesses to what he testified of himself; yet only someone truly upright and sincere, Nicodemus, will become his follower. The first and principal truth of faith is therefore the divinity of Christ, from which all the others flow: faith in the Most Holy Trinity, the truth of all the mysteries of Christ: resurrection, ascension, descent of the Holy Spirit, including the divine motherhood of the Most Holy Mary. This is the faith we must ask for in every prayer, as the Apostles asked Jesus: “We believe, Lord, but increase our faith!” (Luke 17:5).

Holy Family

Tr. pp. 142-143 “Docility to the action of the Spirit… who loved us”

Docility to the action of the Spirit makes us new creatures, transformed into the image of Christ Jesus and ever more aware of living in him, through him, and with him the inheritance he has won for us by offering himself as victim of the new Covenant.

The Father himself illumines this reality of ours through his Word: “The Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if only we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him. I consider that the sufferings of this present time are as nothing compared with the glory to be revealed for us” (Rom 8:16-18).

Since we must therefore share in the suffering of Christ, and since the Father knows our weakness, he does not leave us alone in the effort of identification with the firstborn Son of every man.

“The Spirit too comes to the aid of our weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit itself intercedes with inexpressible groanings. And the one who searches hearts knows what is the intention of the Spirit, because it intercedes for the holy ones according to God’s will. We know that all things work for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those he predestined he also called; and those he called he also justified; and those he justified he also glorified” (Rom 8:26-30).

Mother Rosa believed firmly in God’s plan; therefore she did not spare her life, always hoping, even against all hope, in him, her Good, her strength, and her defender: “Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who acquits us. Who will condemn? It is Christ Jesus who died, rather, was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed intercedes for us. What will separate us from the love of Christ? Will anguish, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?

As it is written: For your sake we are being slain all the day; we are looked upon as sheep to be slaughtered.

No, in all these things we conquer overwhelmingly through him who loved us.”

January 1, Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God

D. pp. 145-147, par. 8

The privilege of Mary, Mother of Grace and Mercy, expresses her dignity and function in the Economy of Salvation: “By conceiving Christ, bringing him forth… suffering with her dying Son, …she cooperated in a wholly singular way in the work of the Savior… to restore supernatural life to souls. For this reason she is a mother to us in the order of grace”; “This motherhood of Mary in the economy of grace continues uninterruptedly… until the eternal fulfillment of all the elect” (LG 61; 62).

Rosa enjoys the gift of the presence of Mary Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae, who reveals her role in relation to the Church and to all humanity: She cooperated in a special way in the work of the Savior with obedience, faith, hope, and ardent charity so that every man might become a son in the Son.

Rosa treasures the presence of the Mother of Grace and Mercy not only in her heart but also in the image.

Mary Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae accompanies her in the development of the work and in her personal journey:

“My angel Bernardo appeared to me with his little Madonna…”;

“Oh Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae! Behold, she appeared to me and assured me of my healing…”;

“She gave me strength…”;

“…behold the little Madonna…! The Child held in his hand a chalice that he wanted to offer me…, and She was holding it. It was a moving sight…, dear Mary conquers” (M. 1.1, p. 83; 5.1, pp. 146-147; 5.1, p. 100).

Mary does not abandon Rosa until the very last moment of her life. Her last greeting is for Mary Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae. The grace and mercy of God mediated by Mary envelop her throughout her life. For her it is experience what for others is an object of faith: “Not only is the dignity of this motherhood unique and unrepeatable in the history of the human race, but unique also is Mary’s participation in the divine plan of man’s salvation through the mystery of the Redemption… The eternal love of the Father comes close to each of us through this Mother…”

January 2

Tr. p. 121 “Yet full… truly children of God”

Yet full liberation of soul and heart is necessary so that the Spirit may make his presence and his continual, delicate inspirations felt like the murmur of a gentle breeze. The Holy Spirit took possession of the soul at baptism and then always with growing abundance through the other sacraments and in a most particular way at the solemn moment of religious profession or of the act of accepting to live according to the spirit and charism of Mother Rosa.

All those who want to follow her spirit and example truly intend to live in fullness the grace of adoption as sons and daughters of God.

Saint Paul warns: “For those who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (Rom 8:14).

January 3

D. pp. 103-105, “The Spirit who bursts in… do not quench the Spirit”

The Spirit who bursts into her as “fire” is, in Rosa’s mystical experience, a constant that enlightens, highlighting the centrality of Love in her relationship with the third Person of the Trinity.

Divine fire evokes various biblical images, expressions of the Spirit’s presence in individuals and in the community: “John is that Elijah who is to come; the fire of the Spirit dwells in him and makes him run ahead of the Lord who comes”; “…on the day of Pentecost… there appeared to them tongues as of fire, which parted and came to rest on each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit…” (Acts 2:1ff.).

Rosa too mystically experiences the Spirit-Love, Fire dwelling in her, and attests its modes in the pages of her spiritual memoirs:

“Oh! you are too sweet…; alas, a fire consumes me… it is… as if I had a furnace”;

“For several days the part of my heart seems as if it wants to open… the fire is burning…”; “…the fire kept growing in me so much that I could not stand on my feet…”; “…I thought I would die of fire; union with my God devoured me so that I had to distract myself so that they would not notice…”;

“The fire devoured me; I felt a something in my left side, so that everything inside me was moving, and this sweetest movement, when it comes, makes me die…” (M. 1.1, p. 120; M. 12, pp. 31; 46; M. 3, pp. 1; 23).

The gift of the Father, the Holy Spirit, did not exhaust his mission in Mary, burning bush of the definitive theophany, full of grace, in whom with the power of his love he formed Jesus. He has continued to be the Love, the power of the life, mission, and resurrection of Jesus, and continues in every person to transmit Trinitarian life and to form in him a child of God.

His action toward Rosa is situated within the horizon of this mission of love: he “indwells” in her, letting himself be experienced mystically as fire and shaping her with this fire into the image of Christ and Mary.

In ecstasies of love he introduces her into the intimacy of his divine essence:

“I spent the night clasped to my Good. Oh! joy! I was dying, so great was the love I felt. Not a single instant did I have outside of him. My Eternal All, who can describe what you do and communicate to the soul and what it experiences in you? Today in you and you for me you live. I feel that I have no other life than yours. A calm, an inner peace that I cannot describe. I speak, or rather I feel… my Spirit. I feel a something that is felt and not seen with bodily eyes, but the intellect sees and understands everything…” (M. 4.3, p. 16).

It is through this divine power that Rosa bears fruit in the Church and for humanity. Letting herself be shaped by the Spirit, she experiences the blessed consequences of his presence, the fruits of his grace: love and peace: synthesis of joy, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22).

The Fire of God — Jesus “will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16), that Spirit of whom Jesus said: “I have come to set the earth on fire, and how I wish it were already blazing!” (Luke 12:49) — is considered by Christian tradition one of the most expressive symbols of the action of the Holy Spirit. For this reason Paul exhorts Christians: “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess 5:19).

January 4

Tr. pp. 32-33 “The mass… forgetting ingratitude”

The mass, the whole, the totality is something abstract, nonexistent, even if there is no lack of a spiritual and moral bond that makes it one family: the human family. Before God, therefore, there is first of all the individual, the person in his unrepeatable singularity.

And since people influence one another for good and for ill, there is no lack of the evil action of the first tempter, the devil, who with serpentine cunning tempts man to evil and works with fierce determination and tireless evil activity to win crowds and nations over to evil.

Hence God’s choice of a people who would remain faithful to him, acting according to his will in view of the coming of the Redeemer. For this purpose he chose Abraham and asked of him an exceptional proof of obedience, commanding him to sacrifice his only son, Isaac. It was truly a supreme human test of “fidelity” to God, almost foreshadowing the supreme test of obedience of the future Redeemer (Gen 22:1-18).

Abraham obeys and God immediately rewards him twofold: sparing his only son and making him father of a people as numerous as the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.

The chosen people will be Israel, one immense family from which the future Redeemer will be born. A people closely united by a promise: the promise of a victory in which the head of the serpent that plunged man into the abyss of guilt, turning the earthly paradise into a valley of tears, will be crushed.

The history of the chosen people thus unfolds from century to century under the guidance of a personal God, one and only, holy and eternal, who makes his divine assistance tangibly felt. He is so close to the people that he manifests with signs and wonders his presence, his will and his word, his paternal governance, strong and merciful; he is a God ready to punish transgressions of the Law he promulgated with authority (I am the Lord), but always patient and ready to forgive, to show mercy, to forget ingratitude (cf. Exod 34:6-9).

January 5

Tr. pp. 101-102, par. 2.5

When we keep in mind our belonging to the Church and are well persuaded that we form one body and one Church with all Christians, then prayer becomes universally choral. If, moreover, we are well convinced that the pilgrim Church and the heavenly Church are also one, then our prayer is surely echoed by the angels and saints of Paradise. A sound foundation is provided by the spiritual patrimony of the Family of the mother of the Immaculate One. “Following the example of Mother Rosa, the Daughters of Saint Anne [and all the members of her spiritual Family], ‘having in view only and above all else God,’ strive to join contemplation with apostolic service and, docile to the Holy Spirit, seek in the intimacy of prayer the encounter with the Father in order to achieve with him, in imitation of Christ, a relationship of tender and intense filial love. Faithful therefore to Jesus’ exhortation to pray without ceasing and taking inspiration from the poor and humble of the Lord, who ‘with groans and sighs, tears and prayers’ (Rule of 1869, 1, 3°) prepared the coming of the Messiah, the Sisters [and Brothers] walk humbly with God (cf. Mic 6:8), seeking his face in the secret of their heart and in the fraternal sharing of a communion of prayer whose center is the Eucharist. In this way, persevering in prayer with Mary, the mother of Jesus, and proclaiming the death and resurrection of the Lord, they prepare with the whole Church his full manifestation: ‘Come, Lord Jesus!’

Wholly devoted to the salvation of the world, a divine work that transcends all human strength and all human wisdom, the Sisters [and Brothers] commit themselves to discovering day by day, in the intimacy of personal and communal dialogue with God, his saving will and to opening themselves to the action of the Spirit in order to become docile instruments of the Father’s mercy” (Constitutions, arts. 48-49). The Constitutions and statutes thus synthesize and translate the thought of the foundress: “I have no other treasure than prayer.”

In the ancient Covenant, Christ himself is the source of prayer; the chosen people looked to him, announced by the Prophets as the future Messiah, a people who in Saint Anne, mother of the Immaculate One, will find the synthesis, empowered by her eminent holiness, as the concentrated conclusion of all the prayers of the patriarchs, prophets, and saints of Israel: “Come and delay no longer!” More than words, theirs was an attitude of continual prayer, the sigh of the heart that in Saint Anne reached the peak of efficacy and intercession.

And she was heard, more than any other person before her, in being chosen as mother of the Mother of the promised Redeemer, of the One who by her immaculate and most powerful prayer would obtain the grace of graces: the descent of the Redeemer to earth, through her own immaculate person, full to the highest degree of every grace and every choicest virtue.

January 6

Tr. pp. 114-115, “The daughters of St. Anne… deliver him from the hand of the wicked!”

The daughters of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family of the holy mother of Mary Immaculate, called to express the Covenant, nourish fraternal communion in hope. Heirs of the communal spirit of the “remnant of Israel,” in which Anne, Joachim, and Mary stand out, constituted in the name of the Lord, faithful to the unity willed by Jesus, reaching toward fraternal love, the emblem of the Family, they live like Mary the dimension of openness to God in all circumstances and situations, with hearts full of attention to brothers and sisters in Jesus Christ.

In the whole history of the Covenant-Hope, love holds a preferential place: “I love the Lord because he has heard my voice in supplication” (Ps 116:1). “As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you… when you see this, your heart shall rejoice” (Isa 66:13-14).

God’s love for his people was realized with the coming of the Messiah in a way beyond all human expectation.

The one who welcomes him first is Mary, the Daughter of Saint Anne.

The Lord, fulfilling his promises in her, luminous dawn of the new era of the world, and through her in her family, where all the hope of the ancient Covenant is contained, gives a response of love to the faithful love of her holy parents Joachim and Anne.

Love rooted in the Covenant, besides making them God’s own, unites them to one another, opening them to the needs of their neighbor: “Defend the lowly and the fatherless; render justice to the afflicted and the needy; rescue the lowly and the poor; deliver them from the hand of the wicked!” (Ps 82:3-4).

January 7

D. pp. 83-84, “Adherence to God… in the ways of God”

Adherence to God, through love, opens the soul to receive a new light. In the new horizon it sees clearly the holiness of God and everything in itself and in others that is out of harmony.

From this light a new tension is born, which causes a suffering all the greater as it makes the soul perceive the intensity of its natural attachments.

Here is how Rosa describes this interior dynamism, the light that illumines her, and the witness of mercy of her Good:

“To suffer and to rejoice. Oh! how useful these lights are to me; in a flash I see everything. Oh! what I feel, how I feel myself all a flame and set about correcting that fault with such force because it is an offense to my Good. Be silent, you heartless ones, why do you offend my dear Crucified One? What has he done to you that you (offend him) so barbarously? I feel so much sorrow, but Jesus is silent. Through the depths of his immense mercy, he suffers and does not punish. Oh! My Love, so many times I beg him to take away this pain I suffer” (M. 1.1, p. 140).

The things Jesus has heard from his Father (cf. John 15:15), and makes known to her in mystical union, must not be forgotten.

They are his words and his divine interventions that weave her personal story and that of the Work. These interventions and words, her Good insists several times, she must set down on paper. Since he is the light of her path, she obeys, even though she cannot foresee that this light will illumine the path of all those who will follow her in the ways of God.
2nd Sunday of Christmas (January 8 to 13)

Epiphany

Tr. p. 54, par. 3.1

The hope that the people chosen by God in the Old Testament lived in the pact of the Covenant, made by God with the Patriarchs, with Moses, and with the Prophets, was founded on the word of God. Hope, the banner of Mother Rosa’s spirituality, is founded on the living and unshakable rock that is Jesus Christ himself.

The people of the new covenant, the Church begotten by the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, walks in hope, awaiting the final glorious manifestation of Christ.

The presence between heaven and earth of an eternal high priest, who is the incarnate Word, cannot fail to have repercussions on humanity. Humanity, reconformed to its Head through redemptive suffering, reconsecrated to the Father by the glory of the Son of Man, constitutes the Church, which is certainly the people of God, but also the new Eve who is born from the side of the new Adam, asleep on the cross in the sleep of a death that conquers death forever.

January 7

Tr. pp. 128-130, par. 3.1

The daughters of Saint Anne and the other members of the Family, awaiting the Lord who comes, build the kingdom in poverty of heart and maternal and paternal self-giving, working in the Church according to a specific mission; they collaborate in the saving work of Christ, carrying in their hearts a single passion: the Kingdom of God and the glory of the Father, following the example of the foundress.

They therefore work for the growth of holy faith, the conversion of sinners, and service to their brothers and sisters, made a sign and instrument of the Father’s merciful love for all people. Inserted in the reality of the local Church, they are in it a leaven of communion, witnesses of hope, and a presence of proclamation, and they build the kingdom in poverty of heart and maternal and paternal self-giving.

As Saint Anne awaited the fulfillment of the promises, the one sent by the Father, so they too, while hoping for the glorious manifestation of the Lord, burning with zeal like Mother Rosa, commit themselves to making him known to the whole world, in the certainty that God has worked, works, and will continue to work great things in people through prayer and our active apostolic work, even when the cross of Jesus, physical or spiritual, invites us to walk, at least in part, the way of Calvary.

It is the cross and the Crucified One that Mother Rosa loved with such ardor and generous devotion, just as the Psalm says: “Lord, my rock, my fortress, my deliverer, my God, my rock of refuge, my shield, my saving horn, my stronghold. The breakers of death surged round about me, the floods of perdition overwhelmed me; the cords of death encompassed me. In my distress I called upon the Lord; in my anguish I cried out to my God; from his temple he heard my voice, my cry reached his ears” (Ps 18:3, 5-7).

January 8

Tr. pp. 131-132, par. 3.3

The daughters of Saint Anne and all who belong to the Family of the Mother of the Immaculate One are called to be a prophetic sign of the merciful love of the Father, of the unconditional offering of Christ Jesus, of hope, fruit of the Spirit.

By their very presence they seek to be credible witnesses for all people, so that they may open themselves to salvation and be able to share in the integral freedom introduced by Christ. Therefore they comfort, help, and make their own the anxieties and concerns of those who suffer; they bring relief to the sick and the marginalized, awakening their hope in the Lord Jesus and in his promises, and help them discover the precious essence of suffering in the light of his passion.
