In the suffering and the marginalized they moreover recognize and serve Christ Crucified, who considers done to himself what is done to the weakest, the most forgotten, and the poorest, and they confidently accompany the hopes of man, directing them toward the path of the covenant that will be definitively fulfilled in the beatific vision, in the splendor of the glory of the Father contemplated for eternity.

To achieve this they follow with watchful readiness the action of the Spirit and work diligently to gather the whole human family around the Father, in the certainty that God alone and his Kingdom are absolute.

Thus, with the whole Church, in prayer and with their hearts, they call out day and night: Come, Lord Jesus!

January 9

Tr. pp. 54-56, par. 3.2

The Church, like Christ himself, is a “mystery,” that is, a manifestation of God who gives himself to the creature. She is the very mystery of the glory of Jesus, considered in the broad, “earthly” sense, but also including the heavenly Church, a marvelous reality like all the works of God.

For these reasons we are not permitted to enter into the knowledge and love of the Son of God, dead and risen, except through knowledge and love of the Church. It is necessary, however, to distinguish the Church as mystical body of Christ, enriched with the Holy Spirit, depositary of the treasures of grace and holiness merited by Jesus Christ (by which she has become his immaculate Bride, called to proclaim Christ to the world and endowed with a prophetic, priestly, and royal spirit), from her other aspects that could obscure her reality. To distinguish is therefore “to clarify.”

A reality that shares in the mystery and holiness of God demands great accuracy and caution of language. The concept of the Church briefly outlined casts, in any case, no shadow on the holiness of the Church herself.

As God in the ancient Covenant willed the most careful construction of the ark, as a sensible expression of the divine holy and sanctifying presence, so Jesus Christ founded the Church as the visible point of reference of his holy and sanctifying presence on earth for the salvation and redemption of men, rich in all the gifts and charisms of the Holy Spirit.

The Church that in the Creed we proclaim holy because of the people who belong to her, who are not holy but are called to holiness, it is wise to distinguish well from the holy and sanctifying Church, icon of the Most Holy Trinity.

To the Church so understood, that is, holy, do not belong sinners who obstinately remain separated from Jesus Christ by sin. They belong to her, however, only virtually, to the extent that they repent and want to return to Christ and live in the bosom of the Church. The Church and Christ, in fact, cannot be sharply separated.

January 10

D. pp. 110-112, par. 5

The Holy Spirit, whom the Father reveals through his mission in time: in creation, in the word of the Prophets, in the Incarnation of the Word in Mary’s womb, in the life of the Son and his work, in the proclamation and work of the Apostles after the glorification of Jesus, fully manifests the fullness of the Trinitarian mystery and continues his work in the mission of the Church.

His mission unfolds from then on in the children adopted by the Father in Christ Jesus.

The life and mission of Rosa, as daughter in the Son, are therefore a mystical place of the Presence and mission of the Spirit.

Her “time” — the stretch of history entrusted by the Father to her — was a time of the Spirit and of witness, but also a time marked by various needs and by trials that did not spare her, a time of vigilance and trusting expectation. On every page of her Memoirs the presence of the Spirit in her life and mission is attested:

“…but he who governs and works in this very work of his knows how to take away and give everything as he pleases… the mental illuminations became much clearer and more vivid for me, so much so that, to my amazement, I hear such sublime words come out of my mouth, and I find everything easy: to preach, to expound and to resolve whatever is asked of me…” (M. 3, P-1).

And on another page she continues the description of this mystical Presence in her life and mission, which turns out to be a wondrous interweaving of the work of the Spirit and of her own participation:

“I feel, and more clearly I see myself guided by my dear Spirit…”;

“I always acted, but I did not know how or why I acted… I did everything, not I, but the one who lives in me: I felt that I was answering and did not know what. I saw everything proceed in order and did not know who ordered it. I, in truth, was not capable, because… a tight crown seemed to encircle my head…” (M. 3, pp. 11; 13).

The Holy Spirit not only works in her, for her, and with her, but also consoles her on her pilgrimage toward the Kingdom with signs and symbols that in the Old and New Testaments foreshadow and reveal his Presence: “One day I was working, I saw a very beautiful Dove coming from above and it seemed to come straight to strike my forehead, but as soon as it grazed me, it vanished. After a few moments a beautiful Light…” (M. 1.1, p. 69f).

In Rosa’s mystical experiences with the Holy Spirit, to the perception of love-living fire, of the gift of understanding, discernment, fortitude (cf. M. 1.1, p. 144; M. 1.2, p. 2; M. 3, p. 11) and of all the other gifts highlighted in her writings, is joined the vision of signs and symbols (light, voice, dove, cloud), which play a specific role in identifying her vocation and particular mission in God’s plan.

January 11

D. pp. 47-48, “The providence she receives… though a small creature”

The providence she receives is for the work that God himself has entrusted to her, especially to console and soothe the suffering of the poor.

Among the providential signs, one expresses the Father’s predilection for the sick:

“…he assigned me to give them a little cloth (to my dear ones during the plague)… anointed with the oil… blessed by the Eternal Father, and to assure them that nothing would happen to them; and so it did” (M. 1.1, p. 40).

The gift of the blessed oil reserved for Christmas Eve, in which God’s lowering of himself to heal the wounds of humanity and restore to it hope and salvation reaches the maximum of participation in our history, undoubtedly affirms the harmony between the divine reality, the symbols that represent it, and the aspect of the mystery of Christ that Rosa must embody in the Church:

“It is two years now that…, on the eve of the birth of the Child Jesus, the Eternal Father himself taught me to prepare a certain oil that he blesses for the sick. What great healings I saw worked, and if they are not healed, he quiets the pain and gives them peace and tranquility of soul to die well” (M. 1.1, p. 69).

The experience described lets us glimpse that the Father sends her to the sick; for this reason he conveys to her his power veiled in matter — a sign that in the Old Testament was regarded as medicine to relieve pain or restore health to the sick, and in the New is also a symbol of the healing power and divine victory over every human infirmity: “Is anyone among you sick? He should summon the presbyters of the Church, and they should pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. The prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed any sins, he will be forgiven” (Jas 5:14-15).

Because of her responsibility toward those she loves, Rosa shares in the divine activity of the Creator, who loves and cares for every creature, however small.

January 12

Tr. pp. 58-59, par. 3.4

Christ, the great prophet, who by the witness of his life and the power of his word proclaimed the kingdom of the Father, fulfills his prophetic office until the full manifestation of his glory (LG 35).

In him all the faithful, made sharers of his mystical body through the outpouring of his Holy Spirit, form a holy and royal priesthood, offer spiritual sacrifices to God through him, and proclaim the praises of the One who called them out of darkness into his wonderful light. There is therefore in the Church no member who has no part in the mission of the whole body, but each of them must sanctify Jesus in his heart and bear witness to him with a spirit of prophecy (cf. PO 2) so that the power of the Gospel may shine forth. The Church is truly a prophetic, priestly people, not only thanks to baptism but also to the Eucharist, where Jesus exercises his eternal priesthood, which is both sacrifice and sacrament. The sacrifice of the Mass is the same sacrifice as the cross.

In the Eucharist Jesus, eternal priest, continues to immolate himself mystically, to exercise his priesthood as head of the Church, his mystical body. Baptism, which makes the Christian holy because it confers sanctifying grace, lays the foundations of Christian perfection and makes the baptized a sharer in the priesthood of Jesus and in his prophetic power. The members of Mother Rosa’s charismatic Family, committing themselves to living their baptism intensely, grow in the prophetic dimension, revealing the saving and merciful love of God, and cooperate with all their strength in the expansion and growth of the Kingdom of Christ in the world, serving Christ in others and leading to him, with humility and patience, all their brothers and sisters (cf. LG 35; 36).

Baptism of the Lord

Tr. pp. 56-58, par. 3.3

The Church is truly the “people of God” to the extent that the baptized belong to Christ Jesus, to his mystical body. Precisely because the Church is identified with the “mystery hidden from the ages in God,” who is Jesus Christ, the reality of the Church, like that of Jesus, is a work of divine wisdom; therefore it is immeasurably superior to our poor human concepts and to our capacity to understand.

The Church is not only the “saved” people, the communion of believers, but also the “saving” universe.

Like Mary, the Church also begets men to a new and immortal life: this is her motherhood in the Holy Spirit (cf. RM 44). To suppose that the sinner as such belongs to her formally, and not virtually, inclines one to think that the Church is sinful, in full contrast with the “holy” Church. It is not for nothing that she is a mystery! The Church, born of the redeeming sacrifice of Christ and the gift of the Holy Spirit, inserts us into Christ through the rite of baptism.

Baptism has always been the outward expression of faith, of incorporation, and of conversion, that is, of the firm decision to renounce the past, sin, radically changing one’s mentality. Only on this condition does one come to belong to the people of God.

The image of the Church as “people of God” must therefore not be isolated from the image of the Church as mystical body and immaculate bride of Christ, as indeed the Council does not isolate it. The Church as mystical body is a word inspired by the Holy Spirit and so it is proclaimed by Saint Paul, and after him by Tradition and the doctors of the Church, in particular Saint Augustine.

Only the image of the Church as mystical body allows us to understand that to detach oneself (through sin) from the Head is to detach oneself from the body, which are the members. In this sense, whoever detaches himself from the Head detaches himself from the members.

The image of the Church as “people of God” has the advantage of opening the door wide also to those who do not belong to her merely virtually, because all men, just as they have the vocation to Jesus Christ, head and king of humanity, so have the vocation to the Church. In this sense, even those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel and the Church but live honestly belong to the soul and not to the body of the Church. And if they live honestly according to the natural moral law written by God in their hearts, the Lord will not fail to come to their aid and save them at the point of death. This truth, however, must not dampen the missionary ardor kindled by Jesus on earth: “Go and preach the Gospel to every creature.” Who can ever calculate the advantage of those who have the grace to live united to Jesus and his immaculate Bride, and the disadvantage of being outside her? “I have come to set the earth on fire, and what do I want but that this fire of truth, of love, and of peace be kindled ever more?” (Luke 12:49).

It is not for nothing that the Church is a “mystery,” and the study of her characteristics occupies one of the most suggestive treatises of Theology.

Season of Lent

Ash Wednesday

Med. of M.R. pp. 7-8

First day of Lent, 1864, in Genoa

This morning my mind was in the desert, where my Good had gone to pray. I begged him to let me remain close to him. Oh, what a sweet union! I felt myself melting, such was the love I felt: so close to my Beloved.

He was praying on his knees, and I felt bitter pain for it. My Love, your suffering is too great! I begged him to give me that pain and let him be relieved. My Good rises. Speak to me, my Love, here there is nothing to give you refreshment. Surely, since it is late, he will try to rest. So it happened: he laid his head upon a stone. No, my Love, take this heart of yours out of this breast of mine, and rest your head on it.

Here I remained absorbed in him, and the conversation lasted long, and, coming to myself again, I found myself always near my Good in the desert. Sweet Love of mine, I feel a sharp anguish: why, my Jesus, are you without anything to shelter you from the weather?

My Sovereign, you, Lord of heaven and earth, for love of me you want to suffer so much.

Turning to the Eternal One, I asked him what I should do to make reparation, and he imposed two things on me to do, and at once I did the penances he told me. When they were finished, I remained absorbed in my God and asked him to arm me with strength and always to keep me with him on the mountain. I prayed to the Most Holy Virgin to obtain for me to consume myself with love.

Thursday

Med. of M.R. pp. 9-10

Always with my God on the mountain. Oh, desert most sweet to me! With you, my Good, I promised to remain there as long as you will be there; I found myself there in an extraordinary way. Always with my Good, and what sweet conversations.

I clasped his feet and such was the union that I truly felt as if I were pressing them to my breast, and weeping I would have dissolved.

Now it seemed to me that he was asking for the salvation of sinners, and I saw him so afflicted. Oh, how I felt sorrow! At the end I asked him to pour grace upon the soul and bathe it, so as to make it grow still more in the flame of his divine Love. It is clear to me at Holy Communion. Oh! my sweet Love!

For a long time I stayed rapt in him, and I was very sorry when this delightful moment ended.

Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 11

Always flying to the desert. My Beloved was praying for sinners; I begged him to offer my whole self as well to the Eternal Father in expiation, and to grant me to suffer all his pains.

My God, how can I free you from the cold? Angels of Heaven, come down and warm the cold limbs of my Good.

Again absorbed in my God, I saw clearly all his sufferings, and felt so much sweetness.

Saturday

Med. of M.R. p. 12

Day 4

As soon as I was recollected — no effort was needed, because everything I had seen and experienced in the desert always remained impressed on my mind — I saw my Good praying to his Eternal Father, and at his feet I would have dissolved in tears, if I could have obtained the gift of them, but my breast was breaking and I could not weep, because I seemed a stone.

My Love, so much suffering: your feet cold and all wounded by the pricks of the stones. I saw how to make reparation for them. I have given you everything: the renewal of my penances, this body, which I beg you to accept as a footstool. It was I who reduced you to this. Once more rapt in him, I passed the hours. Love, destroy me.

1st Sunday of Lent

Med. of M.R. p. 13

Always in the desert. The thought struck me that my Beloved was without any food. How much he will suffer. Yes, my Love, as God you need nothing, but having clothed yourself in human flesh you will surely suffer all the pains to which it is subject.

Only the strength of a God sustains you, because you are the Son of God, and God himself by divinity.

Creatures, is this not enough for you to abandon sin and run to serve, adore, and love God?

Five days have already passed in this dreadful desert. Yes, your strength, which you communicate to me, is here in the highest contemplation. I remained absorbed, and it was also a conversation with my Good, as if I were really near my Savior. At his feet. I contemplated him and felt great sweetness.

My Love, everything is yours and I have nothing.

Monday

Med. of M.R. p. 14

The thought struck me that on that dreadful mountain my Good was suffering the cold, and that the rain was soaking him. I felt the greatest pain. How can I make reparation for such suffering?

Eternal Father, make me become a fire that can dry my Good. How to warm his limbs so numb with cold and water? Eternal Father, give these pains to me, and relieve my Good. Must he still remain on this mountain? Oh, my Love! I shall never be able to suffer with you, to satisfy divine justice, and so, my Savior, will you come down again to your beloved Mother? And here, standing still, I wept.

Tuesday

Med. of M.R. p. 15

Today I remember little. I only feel that I am so happy, because I always seem to be with my Good. It was a union…, better said, contemplation.

He was praying and I was so near. So many affections. I felt a true melting. I prayed when I came back to myself, and made earnest supplications to the Eternal Father; I offered myself as a victim to relieve my sweet Love of his great pains. Then again with him, in him I found myself. Suffering is sweet, it becomes a necessity in order to follow with the beloved in his footsteps.

Wednesday

Med. of M.R. p. 16

My Love, you are alive in this heart of yours, you pervade it entirely. How it grieves me to see you suffer so for ungrateful man and, more than for all, for my ingratitude! Your feet are bloodied because the hardness of the stones broke your most precious flesh. Oh, I want to gather your Most Holy Blood so that no one may trample it. Your holy soles, which are a God’s, reduced to such poverty! Between sorrow and weeping I felt my breast breaking. Eternal Father, I cried, and made a long prayer.

Thursday

Med. of M.R. p. 17

My Father, let me suffer as much as my Beloved suffers. If my sins reduced him so, I want to obtain from you for this reason to suffer with him: all the pains to me. I no longer have life, my life is Jesus, he alone is for me and in me.

Let suffering alone be my food; privations and anguish from now on will be my food and I desire nothing from this earth. Let his torments alone be my friends, my comfort.

Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 18

Without tears, I felt a suffering so strong that it tore at my breast; I felt something I did not understand, but which bound me strongly. My Love, I feel myself fainting, give me the gift of tears so that I can pour out my grief. The thought that you are always on the mountain, alone, without any comfort, joins my suffering, and I feel I cannot bear it. Let me at least see you and hear your Voice. Make me die of love.

Having said this, a union so strong comes about, as if I were near him. I asked him to keep his right hand always upon my head, to direct me, to lead me where he is most pleased, and I told him an infinity of things.

Saturday

Med. of M.R. p. 19

After a thousand words and affections, which lasted a good while, I passed to meditation on the mountain.

Oh, what torment for ungrateful man! I set myself to consider and to speak for my offenders, with earnest promises to do good to my neighbor as much as I could with all my strength; even in the midst of the cruelest sufferings, I would strive to seek the conversion of the poor sinner. Your love for ungrateful man, your suffering for his salvation, moves me to make you vows and firm promises to give myself wholly for the poor sinner…

With earnest promises, with a fire that burned in me more than ever, I repeated: Yes, I will consume myself entirely for the sinner and, if I succeed in saving anyone, I will bring him to your feet, my Love.

2nd Sunday of Lent

Med. of M.R. p. 20

It is Saturday, the day dedicated to the Most Holy Virgin. At once my mind went to the Mother, at the thought of the anguish she must have felt, deprived of her beloved Son. I went to her and, with all the strength of my intellect, I tried to speak to her and said: He suffers; and the Most Holy Virgin was afflicted. I was in such sorrow, and in a flash my mind was with my Dear Jesus on the mountain. Ever steadfast, I asked him many things for the sorrows his Most Holy Mother was suffering. My sweetest Beloved, what pains are these? The mother suffered the Son’s pains, the Son prepared himself wholly to be consumed for the human race.

Monday

Med. of M.R. p. 21

Always on the mountain, and I felt his sufferings vividly. My Love, may I learn to walk well and to pray, to meditate and contemplate always in your Most Holy Presence. May my smallest actions be directed by you, my Love. My Lord and Master, without your guidance I can neither live nor act well, and so I remained absorbed with my Good.

Tuesday

Med. of M.R. p. 22

Always with my mind fixed on my God on the mountain. Today such pain seized me that I could neither speak nor consider anything. All at once I found myself united to my Good and saw everything: his sufferings, and beautiful and sublime lessons. Oh, sweet union! My soul gained much in knowledge and was so strengthened that, returning to my work, I felt neither the pain nor the odor of my sick. It was sweet to serve them, and in my God I felt I did everything.

Wednesday

Med. of M.R. p. 23

My Beloved, always in this desert? When will you come down? How all the sufferings show on your beautiful Face. The thought came to me that soon his delicate hands would be pierced. No, my Love, it will never be; the nails will pierce mine, but never yours; and I wept bitterly, until once more I remained absorbed in my Savior and felt great sweetness.

Thursday

Med. of M.R. p. 24

Still alive in my mind was the nail that was to be driven into his hand, and I kept weeping. I do not want it, and I kept repeating it to him insistently: These delightful hands, pierced by iron? Sweet Love of mine, I feel myself fainting. I entered more deeply into meditation. Your veins will be opened, this flesh will be dragged by the nail into the hole of the Cross. Thus penetrated, I was rapt. He made me feel much that my sorrow pleased him and how I meditated on it.

Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 25

Continuing the contemplation on the torments he suffered, he seemed to me drained of strength. How can he withstand such agony? And I wept bitterly.

I too will remain steadfast in this desert; with you I desire to suffer all your pains. Whatever sorrow oppresses me, I will not cease to remain here, my Good. Only to labor and suffer for you, my Love.

Saturday

Med. of M.R. p. 26

How, cruel ones, will you have the strength to drive nails into these hands of paradise? No, I will hold them tight and, surely, before your hands, they will have to pierce this breast of mine. I felt myself fainting from sorrow, and I offered my anguish: the suffering I bore for sinners.

My thought ran to the thirst my Good suffered in that desert, and I abstained from drinking for 15 days, and then drank a little and at once doubled the abstinence. My Love, how you suffer!

3rd Sunday of Lent

Med. of M.R. p. 27

Throwing myself at his feet, I asked him to let me bathe them with my tears, having no other ointment to offer him and, as with the Magdalene, to accept my sorrow and my tears. I held them tight to my breast, and bathed them with not a few tears.

My Love, forgive me and give me your Love. May I be consumed! So absorbed in my God I remained.

Monday

Med. of M.R. p. 28

Always clasped to his feet, I fainted at the thought that soon they too would be nailed to the Cross. I wept. I seemed to see those feet so vividly, and that the opened veins would have to pour out his Most Precious Blood.

Cruel agony, my God! Your Heart already feels the approach of so terrible an agony, and so absorbed I remained for a long time.

Tuesday

Med. of M.R. p. 29

Always clasped to his Most Holy Feet, from time to time I uttered a word and then wept, and there I stayed.

To me these pains, my God; give me your strength and then with you in suffering, and crucified with you, my God. Come down from this desert, the suffering is too great. How to make reparation for such agony? Then, still, as in a sweet union, I stayed for a long time.

Wednesday

Med. of M.R. p. 30

As soon as I began to meditate, at once my mind went to the desert; I found no words, but a deep sorrow, and silent at his Holy Feet I remained in sweet contemplation, joined to a dull sorrow, so much so that now and then I exclaimed: most sweet and sorrowful feet!

The thought of the meditation was very vivid, in perfect command of feeling materially and of reasoning. Your feet, my Love, I said, will have to undergo martyrdom, and for love of ungrateful man; give everything to me and be relieved, sweet Love of mine. I looked at them and felt deep sorrow.

Thursday

Med. of M.R. p. 31

Always borne in my mind to the feet of my Savior, I remained sorrowful. I raised my gaze, and my thought went to his breast.

I reflected on the most sweet side. You too will have to be fiercely pierced by a lance, and what sorrow the Most Holy Virgin, your beloved Mother, will feel. I considered her agony, I grieved and with sorrowful weeping poured it out at his Holy Feet. My Love, only a God can endure on this mountain. And with tears of deep sorrow I wept at his Most Holy Feet.

Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 32

In flight, with my thought in the desert, always prostrate at his feet, I begged him to make use of me as a footstool, to repair as best I could so much sorrow.

Today I had no words, only a deep melancholy, and so vividly did I have the person of my Savior in my mind that I would have said I was right next to him: I looked at him, I wept, and nothing more.

My Love, you suffer for me, I said, and then I remained in intimate union with my Good. I learned many things and, above all, his Love which consumed me.

Saturday

Med. of M.R. p. 33

My Love, open this breast of yours with that Lance which is to wound you. First, let it pierce me myself and, in some way, let me be pierced by the same sorrow. Yes, my Love, to live with you and to die with you; may your pains always be impressed upon me, and do not permit that any be a trouble to me, but that I love them greatly and suffer with you.

4th Sunday of Lent

Med. of M.R. p. 34

Today, however hard I tried to go to the desert to the feet of my God, I felt nothing, though I was convinced I was flying there, it being the first Friday of March. Dry, a crowd of foolish thoughts carried me here and there. Such sharp sorrow seized me at having been the cause of so much distraction that I felt an agonizing spasm.

Can it be true, my Good, what I have done? I made examinations again, but nothing, and I could not even weep. I was a veritable stump. Do you no longer want me with you, my Love?

An interior Voice told me that he did not like my despair, but that I am always with him. And here I am at his feet, with new promises to do his divine Will perfectly.

Monday

Med. of M.R. p. 35

Wholly absorbed in my Good, I received reproaches because I afflicted myself too keenly, thinking that I was the cause of so painful an aridity. A thousand pains, my God, but hide yourself no more; and I told him all my pains. When I came to the point of telling him that surely I liked being with him, I was dismayed, because his sweetest reproach was enough to cover me with shame.

Tuesday

Med. of M.R. p. 36

I am always with my Good, and today always in the most intimate union. Very clear was my knowledge of all his suffering. A word now and then: to me your suffering; and then I wept without being able to utter a word. Always with him, only in him my whole life.

Wednesday

Med. of M.R. p. 37

I wept prostrate on the ground at the thought of such enormous pains that my Good had to bear. Behold, I rise with a strong impulse and was so united to him that it seemed to me I was very near.

At once my thought runs to the crown of thorns. My Love, your head too will be pierced by thorns, and, entering cruelly into the veins and the skull, they will make you die of pain. So strong and vivid was the sorrow I felt, but it was not enough for me, because I kept repeating to him: to me and not to you this cruel crown.

Thursday

Med. of M.R. p. 38

Gracious hair, in a few days you will be tangled among the thorns of the crown and much of you will be torn out in rage. What agony you will suffer! I feel deeply grieved and I feel, my Love, a true agony, because it is I who so barbarously reduced you. What have I done? At this point I remained absorbed: and what did I feel?

Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 39

Like one who lives only on the sorrow of her beloved, so I found myself. I did every kind of penance and increased them every day. My Love suggested many of them to me and many I devised myself. I asked the Eternal Father whether what I was doing was pleasing to him.

Saturday

Med. of M.R. p. 40

Today I pictured him worn out and still with an infinity of sufferings to bear. How, my Love, will these delicate shoulders of yours be able to bear the enormous weight of the cross? My Eternal Father, no, no, this to me: I alone must carry it, and not my Good. I pictured how he would suffer under that weight and felt all the agony of it. How I see that I am truly nothing, and always so miserable. My God, deign to address a word to me, a glance, and tell me that I shall always be yours, my Love.

5th Sunday of Lent

Med. of M.R. p. 41

Always near my Good, on the mountain of sorrow, I wept and one by one meditated on all the countless sufferings he had to bear. I felt myself torn apart, but a devouring fire came upon me that consumed me, and there were moments when it seemed to me I was being destroyed by that devouring fire. I rejoiced in it immensely, and it was also a terrible and most delicious agony. I felt a great and consoling pleasure in feeling myself destroyed and never would I have wanted it to cease. How sweet it is to die of love!

Monday

Med. of M.R. p. 42

Always in the desert and together with my Good I did penances and fasts, though surely not to remain as he did without tasting anything. Penances to atone for all the gluttony that first I, and then all the human race, commit, and to satisfy divine justice, so that he may lead us onto the sweet path of the new law and free us from the terrible torment of slavery. Love, what reward will you have?

You foresee everything already, and feel true and cruel sorrow. How can I complain of the ingratitude of creatures, when I have done worse toward my God?

Tuesday

Med. of M.R. p. 43

Always with my Good, and today I stayed absorbed in him, receiving graces and great knowledge of the soul. With God, its center, and a portion of the same God, I almost felt no pain, nor could I have a distinct thought: in union nothing can be had within our power, all the faculties are concentrated in God and in his absolute divinity; the soul remains wholly absorbed in his Being.

Wednesday

Med. of M.R. p. 44

Today I felt vividly all his pains, and said many words to him. My Good, I feel my breast breaking with sorrow, I feel myself fainting and, kissing and kissing again his Most Holy Feet, I passed to contemplate his hands, then his breast, his head, and I melted into tears.

Come down from that mountain, your suffering tears me apart, and I cannot bear so great a sight. But, alas, the worst is still to come, with the torments of the tribunal of Caiaphas and Pilate, and the approach of the executioners.

Thursday

Med. of M.R. p. 45

Your flesh, my God, which will be so barbarously torn by thorns, let me repair it; always put me before the scourgings and so you will be spared. But alas, I hear a Voice telling me: “He alone must be the Victim.” So can I do nothing to repair so many cruel torments and fierce scourgings? At least permit me along the way to gather his most precious Blood. My Love, to me alone the suffering.

Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 46

Always near my Good in the desert, and the memory of his passion unfolded point by point in my mind. I wept over it; now I looked at his Holy Feet which, as he climbs the stairs, those with the lances will strike and make bleed from the shoves he will receive. The executioners will offend his delicate limbs. My Love, what agony. I want to prostrate myself on the ground and beg you to walk over this body with your delicate feet.

Saturday

Med. of M.R. p. 47

How your heart will feel great agony! It foresees everything, and feels the sorrow keenly. How can I, my Love, find a way to relieve you of so cruel a torment? How I feel, my Love, a strong desire to suffer. Look at me! When I think that your breast will drip blood, I strive to do penances, but it is a great nothing compared to your sufferings. My Love, it is sweet to suffer for you, my God.

Palm Sunday

Med. of M.R. p. 48

Today, alone with him, the contemplation lasted very little. I was able to meditate much and to know that he was pleased with my penances. I always offered them to him and tried each day to act so that my Good would accept them for the conversion of poor sinners, for whom he made himself a victim of love.

Holy Monday

Med. of M.R. p. 49

The thought of the crowning with thorns suddenly seized me. I stopped to meditate: on your hair which will be woven into a cruel crown of sharp thorns; on the Blood which, from the wounds made by such sharp thorns, will pour over it and run down upon your Breast; my Love, I offer you my head, which has caused you so many pains.

Holy Tuesday

Med. of M.R. p. 50

On the mountain I made him observe my wounds, and told him that I deserved them, but you, my Love, not so; for me you want to suffer thus, my dear Good.

I see that from time to time I faint for lack of strength. Is this a diabolical art? No, he answered me, it is all my grace, the taste you feel in suffering. Sweet Love of mine, my desire to do penance grew ever greater and I tried to do as much as I could.

Holy Wednesday

Med. of M.R. p. 51

My Love, it is so little that I try to make this body suffer compared to the pains you will have to suffer. The thought came to me that my Good will be given gall to drink, and that his lips will be bathed in gall and vinegar. What did I do? I tried to learn to purify my taste.

Holy Thursday

Med. of M.R. p. 52

My Love, always in this desert, drained of strength by so much suffering. Tell me, my Love, have I tried to follow you in sufferings? Send me an Angel, I begged him, to crucify me on the Cross. But I could never obtain any answer; I grieved and wept much.

Good Friday

Med. of M.R. p. 53

What do you think, O my dear Savior, that at last, I hope, you will come down from this desert?

Your sadness makes me understand everything. Holy Wood, purest and most heartfelt Love, who on this Wood is led to die, I feel torn apart, and yet I want to live and die upon that Wood.

Holy Saturday

Med. of M.R. pp. 54-57

Always near my Good in the desert, and I gazed at him fixedly. My mind meditated on his Most Holy Passion and I tried to guess all the pains.

Thinking of the cruel torments to which my Love will be subjected, I said: what shall I do, my Good? I would like to find a way to give you living proof that I too want to suffer with you. I tried to offer him one by one my pains and penances, which I tried more and more to increase.

Today, at last, you will come down from so barbarous a desert and return to your Most Holy Mother. What joy and also sorrow, because you will be able to stay only a little while! But, my Love, do you want to submit even to temptations? This is the last pain you want to give your humanity, which cannot be tempted or have even a hint of temptation.

And yet you permit the ignorant and blind proud devil to think and have the courage to come and tempt your Person. May he be left confounded and ashamed, humbled and, in his pride, muddied. That presumptuous one comes to tempt his Maker, takes on the task and tempts you.

My Love, do you want to suffer even this? It is to teach me that, in battles, trust in you is my victory.

“Love only my God, creatures who seek the good, in him alone is everything and outside him everything is mud.”

Easter: Resurrection of the Lord

FS pp. 63-64, “Oh! What shall I say… outside him everything is mud”

“Oh! what shall I say of the day of the Resurrection? What I felt! I stayed always near the tomb and never tried to eat or to pray. I called him and wanted together with him to be shut in that sepulcher. Risen, I sought him, as the Magdalene did, and having found him, oh! my Love! who can describe what I went through and what I had of yours? I will say it was a continual rapture, always conversing with my God, and so many beautiful lessons and insights I had. Oh! love only my God, creatures who seek the Good! in him alone is everything and outside him everything is mud” (M 2, p. 106f, 122f, 144f, 147f, 186f).

Octave of Easter:

Monday

D. pp. 79-80, “Love impresses on Rosa… grasp them in my mind”

Love impresses on Rosa an interior impulse and moves her toward the Person loved. To be with her Good and to love him is for her superior to any other knowledge and earthly good.

The experience of the Presence of the Beloved is her supreme good. In her Good, with a knowledge that surpasses every human acquisition, she comes to know the prerogatives of her God, which, often unable to transcribe in adequate words, she expresses with a phrase full of wonder:

“…I was carried away by my Good and experienced great things! immense consolation…” (M. 1.1, p. 24).

The act of loving is certainly superior to the act of knowing. From the passage of the Memoirs that follows radiates the experience of a page of the Gospel. It is an example of how knowledge of the mysteries of faith is realized in mysticism:

“On Holy Saturday, from the joy of imagining my Good risen, I exulted. It was a something, stronger than myself, I could not restrain myself, I would have shouted to everyone to come with me to adore my Good who, already beautiful and sweet, was walking about Risen, and to restrain the impulse a little, I began to sing loudly, but it only grew in me. I would have liked to write beautiful things, but I was not able to grasp them in my mind” (M. 1.1, p. 21).

Tuesday

D. p. 80, “The act of love is certainly… contemplative to the divine life”

The act of loving is certainly superior to the act of knowing. From the passage of the Memoirs that follows radiates the experience of a page of the Gospel. It is an example of how knowledge of the mysteries of faith is realized in mysticism: “On Holy Saturday, from the joy of imagining my Good risen, I exulted. It was a something, stronger than myself, I could not restrain myself, I would have shouted to everyone to come with me to adore my Good who, already beautiful and sweet, was walking about Risen, and to restrain the impulse a little, I began to sing loudly, but it only grew in me. I would have liked to write beautiful things, but I was not able to grasp them in my mind” (M. 1.1, p. 21).

Mystical experience is not limited to the contemplative gaze toward God, but is a process of interior transformation. The relationship with God or with the mystery of salvation leads to an immediate participation of the contemplative in the divine life.

Wednesday

FS pp. 209-210 “The crucified Redeemer… Virgin Mary”

The crucified Redeemer is the mediator before the Father. Mother Rosa has unlimited trust in the power of intercession of the blood of the Mediator of the new Covenant, which speaks more eloquently than that of Abel (Heb 12:24): “Only the blood of my dear Crucified One can do all things with the heart of his eternal Father: knock and do not tire, and it will be opened to you” (Letter to Emilia di Fitalia: 3/5/1885).

Her Christ-centered piety is not confined to the cross and the sufferings of the Savior. Accustomed to living the paschal mystery in its integrity, she rejoices intensely in contemplating the triumph of the Risen One each year, after having mystically shared in the whole Passion on Good Friday.

On Holy Saturday of 1862 she lived the jubilation of Jesus’ resurrection to such a degree that she could not contain herself for joy and, to restrain the impulse, began to sing (M 1.1, p. 21). On Easter Sunday of 1866 she had a vision of the feast being celebrated in heaven, after which she gave vent to her jubilation with an ardent prayer to the risen Lord, to the eternal Father, to the Holy Spirit, to the Virgin Mary (M 1.1, p. 37f).

Thursday

D. pp. 54-55, “The aspects of the mystery of Christ… in my poor room”

The aspects of the mystery of Christ most evident in Mother Rosa’s mysticism are Love, the constant and glorious Presence, self-emptying: “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross” (Phil 2:8).

Jesus makes himself visible to her in the inseparable reality: love-cross. Her soul is pierced by the great mystery of our salvation: “He was handed over for our transgressions and was raised for our justification” (Rom 4:25).

The Love of Christ for the Church: “Christ loved the Church and handed himself over for her” (Eph 5:25) becomes, in her mystical experience, an event that transforms and sanctifies her.

Her love, in fact, ever more total and exclusive for her Crucified Good is evident in what she writes:

“While I was about to begin the meditation I found myself before the wound of the right foot of my Good, dripping blood. Oh! what I felt, I remained absorbed in him, I cannot say for how long! I saw nothing then, I only felt a sharp pain and it seemed to me so intense that I could not bear it. Oh! My Love! what I did not feel, afterward, when I came back to myself! only you could say” (M. 1.1, p. 35).

The union that holds her bound to him sharpens her hearing to listen to his Voice: “Whoever wishes to come after me must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). And in the harmony between the divine Presence that imposes itself and her own personal commitment, she is led to experience the love and the sorrow present in every wound of the Divine Body of the Redeemer and Savior of humanity:

“Rapt again, I find myself near the Side of my Beloved and what I felt…”

“Only when I have afflictions and tribulations do I feel a relief, because I feel this fire less. Oh! what a thirst I have to suffer, I feel no sorrow at all, because the thirst to suffer is without equal! it is sweet to suffer for the beloved!

On the 7th I had a something in meditation that carried me away, and I remained as if I were near the wound of the shoulder. Oh! My Love, afterward I learned to say: with my tears I will wash this wound and suck out its humor. Oh! at once a flood of tears came to me and, as if truly with my mouth I could suck that balm, I came to myself and found myself full of strength, whereas before I had been worn out by the labors done for the sick and the poor whom I went to help; I felt almost faint when I returned to my poor room” (M. 1.1, pp. 41; 58-59).

Friday

D. p. 101, “…I saw the face of my… is the sight of the Redeemer”

“…I saw the face of my Redeemer. Oh! how beautiful it was! What joy, my love! It was so luminous that I would not know how to explain its light and beauty. I felt wholly inflamed by that object which consumed me. Ah! when will be that day when in so beautiful a moment you, O my Good, will consume me?” (M. 1.1, p. 13).

The Spirit draws her to Jesus: he awakens in her like a devouring fire, but what in turn arouses this power of love is the sight of the Redeemer.

Saturday

FS 256-258, “The heart of Rosa Gattorno… to see God loved by all”

The heart of Rosa Gattorno was a volcano in constant activity, insatiable for love. Here is an outpouring of hers in a letter to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

“I would like to draw the whole world, to give to all, to feed all. Oh! if from my veins I could make gold flow for the poor! Do you know what I would do? By myself, vein by vein, I would want to draw it out until they were dry. Oh! would I be satisfied? No! it is too ardent!…” (Undated letter, no. 76).

One could compose a fine anthology from the effusions of her longing to make her dear Good known and loved, which leap out in the pages of her spiritual diary. Here are some:

“My Good, what can I do to make you known to the whole world? Oh! how many there are who do not know you! and those who have known you flee from you for never having seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry out loudly that all come to love you” (Year 1862: M 1.1, p. 30).

“Oh! why do all not love you? Do you see, O my Good, the burning thirst I have to save souls?” (M 1.1, p. 33).

“O my Love! make use once of this miserable instrument of yours to revive the faith and the conversion of sinners!”

— “All souls, come! Ah! love Jesus, do not offend him!… I would have run through all the streets crying out that they should love Jesus. I threw myself face down on the ground and asked the eternal Father loudly to let me die a martyr to save the souls redeemed by him. Am I not your instrument? (Year 1867: M 1.1, pp. 60, 119).

“O my Love! how I feel myself burning with desire to make you known and loved by all! May your name be blessed by all tongues. My God! Oh! if I could make everyone feel what I feel!” (M 1.2, p. 87).

Many of these outpourings are entrusted to paper after some of her most intimate experiences of the great mysteries communicated to her with infused light. She then thinks that many others could share in such a good. On the feast of the Resurrection of 1863, after a vision that filled her with consolation, she wrote: “O Love! why do you not let the unbelievers see a little of it?” (M 1.1, p. 186f).

She often expresses her longing to go through the world converting sinners, to suffer for them, to die a martyr for the salvation of the world, to see God loved by all.

2nd Sunday of Easter

Tr. p. 101, “When we keep in mind… Come, Lord Jesus!”

When we keep in mind our belonging to the Church and are well persuaded that we form one body and one Church with all Christians, then prayer becomes universally choral. If, moreover, we are well convinced that the pilgrim Church and the heavenly Church are also one, then our prayer is surely echoed by the angels and saints of Paradise. A sound foundation is provided by the spiritual patrimony of the Family of the mother of the Immaculate One. “Following the example of Mother Rosa, the Daughters of Saint Anne [and all the members of her spiritual Family], ‘having in view only and above all else God,’ strive to join contemplation with apostolic service and, docile to the Holy Spirit, seek in the intimacy of prayer the encounter with the Father in order to achieve with him, in imitation of Christ, a relationship of tender and intense filial love. Faithful therefore to Jesus’ exhortation to pray without ceasing and taking inspiration from the poor and humble of the Lord, who ‘with groans and sighs, tears and prayers’ (Rule of 1869, 1, 3°) prepared the coming of the Messiah, the Sisters [and Brothers] walk humbly with God (cf. Mic 6:8), seeking his face in the secret of their heart and in the fraternal sharing of a communion of prayer whose center is the Eucharist. In this way, persevering in prayer with Mary, the mother of Jesus, and proclaiming the death and resurrection of the Lord, they prepare with the whole Church his full manifestation: ‘Come, Lord Jesus!’”

Monday

D. pp. 103-104 “The Spirit who bursts in… image of Christ and Mary”

The Spirit who bursts into her as “fire” is, in Rosa’s mystical experience, a constant that enlightens, highlighting the centrality of Love in her relationship with the third Person of the Trinity.

Divine fire evokes various biblical images, expressions of the Spirit’s presence in individuals and in the community: “John is that Elijah who is to come; the fire of the Spirit dwells in him and makes him run ahead of the Lord who comes”; “…on the day of Pentecost… there appeared to them tongues as of fire, which parted and came to rest on each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit…” (Acts 2:1ff.). Rosa too mystically experiences the Spirit-Love, Fire dwelling in her, and attests its modes in the pages of her spiritual memoirs:

“Oh! you are too sweet…; alas, a fire consumes me… it is… as if I had a furnace”;

“For several days the part of my heart seems as if it wants to open… the fire is burning…”;

“…the fire kept growing in me so much that I could not stand on my feet…”;

“…I thought I would die of fire; union with my God devoured me so that I had to distract myself so that they would not notice…”;

“The fire devoured me; I felt a something in my left side, so that everything inside me was moving, and this sweetest movement, when it comes, makes me die…” (M. 1.1, p. 120; M. 12, pp. 31; 46; M. 3, pp. 1; 23).

The gift of the Father, the Holy Spirit, did not exhaust his mission in Mary, burning bush of the definitive theophany, full of grace, in whom with the power of his love he formed Jesus. He has continued to be the Love, the power of the life, mission, and resurrection of Jesus, and continues in every person to transmit Trinitarian life and to form in him a child of God.

His action toward Rosa is situated within the horizon of this mission of love: he “indwells” in her, letting himself be experienced mystically as fire and shaping her with this fire into the image of Christ and Mary.

Tuesday

Tr. pp. 148-149, “The outpouring of the Spirit… we are invited to meditate”

The outpouring of the Holy Spirit gives rise to the new and renewing reality of the Church, depositary of the work of redemption, guardian of the merits of Jesus, inexhaustible source of the descent of the Holy Spirit with all the richness of his gifts.

The outpouring of the Spirit unifies the Church, making of the “people of God” one body, the “mystical body of Jesus,” the total Christ.

Baptism makes all the baptized members of a single body.

In all the Sacraments the Holy Spirit works for the unity of the Church, especially in the Eucharist, which is at once consecration and transcendence of the world. Consecration, because it is an earthly gesture on poor earthly things that are woven into our daily existence. Transcendence, because the Eucharist places in our earthly condition a foretaste of the heavenly condition and transforms the community of believers gathered with Christ at the altar into a community above time, immersed in the mystery, set on the plane of the Parousia, that is, of Jesus’ coming in glory. We are therefore not permitted to grow in the love of the Son of God except through knowledge and love of the Church. The Church and Christ are not adequately distinct. The Church, in fact, is identified with the “mystery hidden from the ages in God.” Therefore her reality, like that of the glorified Jesus, is in harmony with the divine wisdom that conceived her, and so exceeds our capacity to understand. For this reason we must not be surprised if we have to use a multiplicity of concepts, all merely approximate, which at times seem almost to conflict with one another. In fact it is a matter of the mysterious richness of her reality, which we are invited to meditate upon.

Wednesday

FS p. 205, “Jesus Christ the Beloved… in her letters”

One could almost speak of a certain theocentrism in the spirituality of Rosa Gattorno. In reality, however, her piety, which is faith and love, opens with all its impetus to the Incarnate God, her beloved Spouse, her Beloved, as she likes to call him. In the affectionate meditations of Lent 1864 we have a testimony of the intensity of her love for Jesus, specifically for the suffering Jesus (M 2, pp. 77-187). But on every page of her Memoirs, in every letter of hers, Jesus appears as the object of her love, the center of her life.

“When one has Jesus, one has the whole world.”

— “To grow in the spirit and love of Jesus”: this is the ideal of every daughter of St. Anne (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 12/16/1868, 10/1/1869; Circ. 1886). She would have wanted all of them enamored, mad for sweet Jesus.

“If you knew how much Jesus loves you — she wrote to a postulant — surely, mad, you would be his and would do nothing else than press him to your heart and say to him: Speak to me, command me!” (Letter to Caterina Rapallino: 1868).

“To live for Jesus,” “to see Jesus in everything,” are frequent recommendations in her letters.

Thursday

D. pp. 74-75, “The choice of the Beloved… is always with me”

The choice of the Beloved and of his kingdom does not spare Rosa tribulations and slander. The Gospel imperative: “Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life” (John 12:25) is impressed by the Spirit like a seal on her heart.

The eighth beatitude proclaimed by Matthew: “Blessed are they who are persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (5:10)” is like an understanding of love with the Beloved to remain in him and enjoy his consolations:

“My interior rejoices, my soul exults (in tribulations and slander) with consolation, and I feel a peace without equal. Oh! My Love! Many things I saw in these days and my Beloved assured me that soon I will have great consolations.”

“I find myself in the most horrible spiritual pains, which for me are the greatest, because I do not find, I do not see my Beloved, for several days now I have not heard his delightful Voice. Alas! what have I done, my Love, who are my life. My Eternal Father, do not abandon me! Come, tell me what I have done. Ah! no, a thousand torments but not these. The others were of a most horrible kind. Alone! Jesus, you know it, I have only you, who leave me in this state, I die of sorrow; behold, my Love is with me. Oh! how many caresses he gave me! it would take too long to describe them: union, raptures, light to see those who tormented me, why they did it, who had moved them to do it!” (M. 1.1, pp. 77; 126).

Rosa’s experience would not have been possible if God himself had not willed, guided, and sustained it. She opens her heart to the absolute benevolence of the Beloved, abandons herself in him, accepts his unlimited demands: she meets divine love and is filled with graces.

In the Beloved she finds synthesized all the love of the Father and of the Spirit for her. Dwelling in the Beloved, who is the perfect response of love to the Father, she enjoys the certainty of being pleasing to him.

She cannot refuse the Beloved what he asks of her:

“My Beloved keeps suggesting new sufferings to me, how I should do to afflict myself more. I have no thought that is earthly, I work, I act because my Good is always with me.

Friday

D. pp. 83-85, par. 3

The Voice again with its usual sweetness: try it, it is my desire, and then I said, no, this Voice is my Good because I know it too well, and the ugly one who speaks to me secretly is the dragon. And at once I set to it, indeed I made those irons myself and then put them on. They had on a skin most atrocious points and I felt nothing, not even that night, they were sweetest pains. Oh! sweet Love, what did I receive as a gift? Oh! sweetness (rapt in Him I enjoyed the most beautiful and dear delights, illuminations) he taught me so many beautiful things” (M. 1.1, p. 138).

Adherence to God, through love, opens the soul to receive a new light. In the new horizon she sees clearly the holiness of God and everything in her and in others that is out of harmony.

From this light is born a new tension that causes a suffering all the greater in that it makes the soul perceive the intensity of its natural attachments.

Here is how Rosa describes this interior dynamism, the light that enlightens her and the witness of mercy of her Good: “To suffer and to rejoice. Oh! how useful these lights are to me, in a flash I see everything. Oh! what I feel, how I feel myself all a flame and I set about correcting that defect with such force because it is an offense to my Good. Be silent, heartless ones, why do you offend my dear Crucified One? What has he done to you that you (offend him) so barbarously? I feel so much sorrow, but Jesus is silent. Through the depths of his immense mercy, he suffers and does not punish. Oh! my Love, so many times I beg him to take from me this pain that I suffer” (M. 1.1, p. 140).

The things that Jesus has heard from his Father (cf. John 15:15), and which he makes known to her in mystical union, must not be forgotten.

They are his words and his divine interventions that weave her personal story and that of the Work. These interventions and words, her Good insists several times, she must set down on paper. Because he is the light of her path, she obeys even though she cannot foresee that this light will illuminate the path of all those who will follow her in the ways of God.

From her own testimony on this we receive confirmation:

“All for my Good, and so I spent many days and months without writing, but for this he gave me a just reproach, yet so gentle and sweet that I did not know what to answer, only: forgive me, my Good. - Tell me why you do not write? - Oh! my Love, how can I? - At night half an hour for a note and then in time you will resume. - Oh! sweetness without equal, yes, my Good, I will not delay in doing it” (M. 1.1, p. 155).

Thanks to these written sources, born of obedience to Jesus, we are enabled to reconstruct the authentic story of Rosa with her Good and Lord. It is a profession of faith in him present in history, through which he continues to manifest himself to those who develop the capacity to perceive and contemplate his Presence.

Saturday

TC pp. 321-323 “How that consoled me!… Oh my Savior!”

How that consoled me! But my voice:

- Take the smallest one and put a sail on it; and then do not worry about where you will go!

Having carried out at once what I was ordered, I took the smallest and, having put the sail on it, tried immediately to get to the helm. I hoped to find my God, but not only was he not there, there was not even a helm. Without a thought, I saw myself carried by the wind to the open sea; every moment I seemed to be submerged in the waves, but I feared nothing. I prayed when I saw myself almost lost: My God, if the boat sinks, you will make me walk on the water as you did with Peter; would you give me your hand too? (cf. Matt 14:28-31). And I kept on.

Finally, tossed this way and that, I see that it takes the course of a very large river. Having entered it, there were so many beautiful ships and little boats: and I in that tattered ship! As I passed near them, all the owners mocked me, and I laughed. One shouts at me, seeing me advance like that and make my own way:

- Where are you going?

What was I to say?

- Where my Master sends me!

- Having said that, he heaps insults on me:

- Insolent one, turn back!

- I cannot: my Lord sends me here!

Worse! he gets angry:

- She comes from far away with nothing, and then she will want bread. We will not give her any: we help only our own, not strangers.

- Have pity! I ask you for nothing and will not ask. This very poor little boat will give you no trouble: I will tie it to one of those rocks.

Grumbling, he was persuaded. Another, kinder but very curious, wanted to know how I had managed to arrive in that manner, in so ruined a boat, without a helm, with a sail all in rags. He looks inside and sees no provisions.

- How will it be? She says she asks for nothing: how will she manage? - he said this under his breath, but clearly enough to be heard.

Having tied the boat up well, as best I knew how, I tried to make my way to my Good in the great temple, to his Vicar. Oh! what a surprise! Looking so shabby, ragged as I was, a poor slave of the Lord kisses the foot and hand of his Vicar. Oh! most humble Sovereign! Oh mercy of God! He asks her about the little ship, wants it near him and prophesies its future. Oh my Savior!

3rd Sunday of Easter

FS p. 257, “One could compose… what I feel”

One could compose a fine anthology from the effusions of her longing to make her dear Good known and loved, which leap out in the pages of her spiritual diary. Here are some:

“My Good, what can I do to make you known to the whole world? Oh! how many there are who do not know you! and those who have known you flee from you for never having seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry out loudly that all come to love you” (Year 1862: M 1.1, p. 30).

“Oh! why do all not love you? Do you see, O my Good, the burning thirst I have to save souls?” (M 1.1, p. 33).

“O my Love! make use once of this miserable instrument of yours to revive the faith and the conversion of sinners!”

- “All souls, come! Ah! love Jesus, do not offend him!… I would have run through all the streets crying out that they should love Jesus. I threw myself face down on the ground and asked the eternal Father loudly to let me die a martyr to save the souls redeemed by him. Am I not your instrument? (Year 1867: M 1.1, pp. 60, 119).

“O my Love! how I feel myself burning with desire to make you known and loved by all! May your name be blessed by all tongues. My God! Oh! if I could make everyone feel what I feel!” (M 1.2, p. 87).

Monday

FS p. 180, “External tribulations hidden personal interests”

Setbacks, misunderstandings, and persecutions are the normal patrimony of all who commit themselves to following Christ. The life of Rosa Gattorno could not be an exception. From the time she accepted, by God’s will, her mission as foundress, she understood that it is the mark of every evangelical undertaking to have to face, first of all, the postulates of human prudence and then the opposition, not only of the enemies of the interests of the Kingdom, but also of the good and well-intentioned who do not share or understand the viewpoints of one who acts under the divine impulse.

She was conscious of being an instrument of God, though an unskilled one: her foundation was the Work of God. It is no wonder that in every opponent she saw an adversary of God’s plan, even an unwitting collaborator of the evil one. Hence her deep suffering, especially when she discovered in her opponents hypocrisy, ulterior motives, and hidden personal interests.

Tuesday

D. pp. 89-91, par. 2

What we believe by faith: that Jesus is truly and mysteriously present in the natural elements of bread and wine, is, for Rosa, an object of experience:

“One morning, as I was receiving the Most Holy Flesh of my Love, I felt a taste so exquisite that I would not know how to explain it… it brought me an indescribable consolation” (M. 1.1, p. 18).

It is a vital necessity for Rosa to take part daily in the Eucharistic Table, where she is nourished with the Body and Blood of Christ, which strengthens and sustains her especially in the moments of struggle of the spirit when she remains alone with him: “Only the strength that Jesus provided me of being able every day to feed on the Heavenly Bread…”

“I went to receive Holy Communion. What did I feel, my Good,… I remained absorbed in him…, on coming to myself, I was so comforted, strong as a giant, I would have defied the whole world, persecutions…” (M. 1.1, p. 9; 142).

From him, who chose to use as matter and symbol the elements that recall not only the primary nourishment of life but also the sharing of bread with the poor, she learns to love those who are alone and suffer: she burns with desire to share with others the life she experiences in prayer:

“…in haste I ran to church to receive him. Oh! what I felt! Say, my Good, only you could say. Oh! you who are my Paradise! What can I do to make you known to the whole world? Oh how many there are who do not know you and those who know you flee from you for never having seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry out loudly that all come to love you” (M. 1.1, p. 30).

In this desire for radical self-giving she anticipates what in the Eucharist matures over time: to make concrete the aims intrinsic to the Sacrament of the paschal mystery: “to make of all people one Family.”

In her participation in the Eucharist she unifies her whole life, which is transformed into “light and salt of the earth,” helping to give its true face of love to a world disfigured by evil. It is this real participation, this effective sacrifice of her person, that allows Christ not to be confused with the sacrament, but rather to reveal himself through the Sacrament as Eternal Presence walking with humanity.

Rosa, in fact, in the sacrament unites herself to the presence, learning to live in God and for God alone.

Wednesday

FS pp. 65-66 “As the invasion… who would act and live continually”

As the invasion of the divine made itself felt in her spirit, Rosa felt herself ever more purified, lightened of the impediments that hindered her impulse toward the supreme Good. Here is how she describes, in the book Trials and Comforts, the effect of those passive purifications, in a beautiful page worthy of the great masters of mysticism:

“My Crucified One subdues the humanity, gives it vigor and energy, strengthens the spirit which, victorious, rules over all the powers, which are thus so well subject.

Self-love dissipates, is lost, vanishes, so much that even one’s own name is forgotten. Pride is conquered and is looked upon as an instrument of scorn, as an enemy. One feels great pleasures and great consolation when one sees them crushed.

The will, which is overbearing, grows quiet. My Crucified One has exchanged my will for his, and it is infinitely sweet and pleasant no longer to possess it. Oh! how it would have rebelled, had he not nailed it down, while leaving it always free!” (TC, p. 3f).

With the same capacity for self-analysis, though in her own way, she describes the various ways in which she experiences the intimate presence of God and his communications: infused recollection, simple gaze of love, interior invitations, languors of love… She knows that none of this is the fruit of her own effort, but that all is pure gift of God, the experience of a life that is not her own. To express such newness she very often appropriates the well-known text of Saint Paul: It is no longer I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me (cf. Gal 2:20). She writes in 1867:

“Such was the union with my God that, as soon as I began to pray, at once I was absorbed in him; and I always saw new things… He taught me, corrected me, made me see how I should do his work…, as if I did not live, but there were in me a person who acted and lived continually for me.

Thursday

FS p. 203, “In everything and for everything the will of God… I would feel nothing”

In the book Trials and Comforts Mother Rosa imagines a lively dialogue with a “shepherd” who would like to dissuade her from going on, since she is walking off the road. She answers every insinuation: “I will do nothing else but the will of God!”

Finally the “shepherd” says to her, annoyed:

“Oh! what a head! your very speech is that of an ignorant creature.” To which she replies: “You are right, I have no other science than the will of my Lord!” (TC, pp. 365-367).

Here is the pivot of her spirituality, and also the cause of her inner anguish, having to face for so many years, alone, the uncertainties of her interior life and the decisions concerning her responsibility as foundress: will it be God’s will? This torment, as we have already seen, is present in many pages of her spiritual diary. God’s will, God’s pleasure, God’s good pleasure, God’s approval, are synonyms that are also at the center of her pedagogy with the sisters:

“If you knew what consolation I feel just in pronouncing this word - God’s pleasure - and even more, if the sweet thought of being or of being able to come to his delight awakens vividly in me! I feel entirely beside myself, so that if I had to face the cruelest martyrdom, I would feel nothing…” (Letter to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: P. 204, 2/4/1871).

Friday

FS pp. 259-260, “what matters… very little good”

What matters is, first of all, to evangelize with one’s life (Circ. Letter 8/20/1895). One of the sisters testifies at the informative process: “She wanted and required us to be missionaries in the hospitals, first by our bearing and then by charity and, finally, by word” (Summ., p. 650).

Mother Rosa’s apostolic heart knew two moments of deep joy: one, when she gave her maternal embrace to the sixteen sisters of the first expedition that left for Latin America on November 23, 1878, a harbinger of rapid expansion on that continent; and the other, that day when she presented to Leo XIII the four members of the first mission to East Africa, in November 1886.

In her numerous letters to the missionary sisters one feels her heart throb as with a holy envy of the good fortune they enjoy of being able to toil and suffer in the vanguard of the Kingdom of God. She would have wanted to have so many daughters of St. Anne as to be able to satisfy all the requests that reached her. She wrote to the superior in Eritrea, Sr. A. Pierina Della Valle:

“My God, what a pain not to have sisters!… Come, courage! I wish I were ten years younger and had strength; I would go and become a cobbler! But I am very old and always very little well” (Letter of 11/8/1895).

Saturday

D. pp. 69-70, par. 4

Infinite Wisdom makes her a sharer in his Light which penetrates the hearts of men, scrutinizes them, shakes them, converts them:

“He let me see into certain hearts and said this to me: every time you need to see them and penetrate them, you will see them. Thus whatever you ask of me for the good of the souls who are with you and whom you care for, I will give you all. Likewise for what you desire for the Priests, that very thing which through prayer you want me to give them, I will give them. You will distinguish clearly the good from the bad; I will make you feel a revulsion when they have indecent ideas against chastity. You will feel it at once and be warned. Do not doubt that I will always be near you, there are many… Oh! what pain… that I felt. Likewise for the false devout women you will have special lights to distinguish them well…” (M. 1.1, p. 63).

She receives most beautiful instructions on the love that Jesus bears for man, while man responds so poorly:

“Oh! my Beloved! Oh! Yes, I see well how much you love creatures, and how poorly they respond to you. You are all love for them! A Voice answered me, yes, I love man immensely, and as he said this to me he drew near me” (M. 1.1, p. 152).

New lights project her toward the future with optimism and hope. She need not fear because there is One who guides her, sustains her, and plans for her:

“At night he came to console me. He let me see what will happen at my death, what they will do with me, how they will dress me, and who will have influence over it; there will be one who will have my last direction, who will live in obedience, but will take care not to command me things that she has not first felt well within herself, the Tertiary habit will be my habit, and the rest of St. Anne” (M. 11, p. 164).

With the expert guidance of her Master she sees the various aspects of her path in following the Poor Christ. Jesus gradually shows her, walking with her, how to cooperate in the work of redemption.

He forms her for penitent conversion, for engaging in the struggle with the evil one by overcoming him with unconditional faith in her Lord, for being a victim of love to create a counterweight in the divine justice provoked by our sins, for bringing sinners to salvation.

4th Sunday of Easter

Tr. pp. 150-151, “The Church, that is, the Kingdom… clothed in glory”

The Church, that is, the kingdom of Christ already present in mystery by the power of God, grows visibly in the world. This beginning and this growth are signified by the blood and water that flowed from the opened side of the crucified Christ and are foretold by the Lord’s words about his death on the cross: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all to myself” (John 12:32). Every time the sacrifice of the cross “by which Christ our Paschal Lamb has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7) is celebrated on the altar, the work of our redemption is renewed. And together with the sacrament of the Eucharistic bread, the unity of the faithful who form one body in Christ, who is the light of the world, is represented and brought about; from him we come, through him we live, toward him we are directed” (LG 3).

In this truly marvelous sense Jesus is our hope and the Church is truly the Ark of the Covenant, prefigured in the old Covenant, divinely realized in the new and eternal Covenant.

The Church is therefore the beginning on earth of the kingdom of Christ and of God.

In the light of this splendid theology of the Church the various images of the Church outlined by the Council are luminously understood: “the Church is the sheepfold whose one door is Christ; it is the flock of which Christ himself is the Good Shepherd and prince of shepherds; it is the field of God in which the ancient olive tree grows, whose holy root were the patriarchs…; the Church is the building of God of which the Lord is the cornerstone, the foundation on which the Church itself is built and from which it will receive stability and cohesion. The Church is the house where his family dwells, the dwelling of God with men; it is the new Jerusalem, the Holy City. In it, as living stones, we form a spiritual temple. This holy city Saint John, in the Apocalypse, contemplates in its final phase, coming down from God as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:1ff.).

The Church is the heavenly Jerusalem, “our mother,” the immaculate bride of the immaculate lamb.

And while the Church accomplishes on this earth her pilgrimage far from the Lord (cf. 2 Cor 5:6), she is like an exile who seeks and desires the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, until with her Spouse she will appear clothed in glory (cf. Col 3:1-4)” (cf. LG 6, 7).

Monday

FS pp. 258-259, “O Love… and you were his echo, another”

“O Love! why do you not let the unbelievers see a little of it?” (M 1.1, p. 186f).

She often expresses her longing to go through the world converting sinners, to suffer for them, to die a martyr for the salvation of the world, to see God loved by all.

At the moment of presenting the text of the Rules to the Pope, June 1871, while a shadow of harsh uncertainty weighed on her spirit, a joyful future of missionary splendor surfaced on the horizon of her faith:

“This horizon seems very dark to me for us, but the right hand of our eternal Father in an instant can dispel everything and the Daughters of St. Anne Mother of the Immaculate enjoy the most beautiful light in all of Catholicism and bring it to shine in the most idolatrous countries, and there plant the standard of St. Anne!” (Letter to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 6/2/1871).

She would like to make of every daughter of St. Anne a spokeswoman of Jesus to let all people hear the message of the Love that saves; that all would have the gift she experiences when she feels herself the pure instrument of the One who makes her speak.

She wrote to her intimate Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

“Jesus will put on your tongue words that you yourself will not know how you pronounced them… Love, and think that it was Jesus who spoke in your heart and you were his echo, another” (Undated letter, no. 76).

Tuesday

FS pp. 35-36, “The secret of true joy… Nothing, nothing!”

The secret of “true joy” she had learned in the school of Francis of Assisi, discovering it precisely in contempt and adversity.

She wrote, in confidence, to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa:

“Daughter, courage! for to die upon the cross one needs strength and resignation. I have no rest day or night: always at the table writing from morning to night, thoughts upon thoughts, labors upon labors, on every side I find cruel thorns…; but always cheerful and always resigned: so my Jesus teaches me” (3/13/1872).

It was her teaching to the sisters, as appears repeatedly in the letters:

“You will tell all my daughters to be cheerful, as their Mother is”

- “Cheerful, my little daughter, if you want to become a saint!”

- “My dear, cheerful! do you understand?”

- “Why do you cry? That is for children. Come! be cheerful!”

- “Be cheerful, and live!”

- “Be cheerful! all the rest we will put into the heart of God the Father”

- “In prosperity as in adversity, always joyful; because in adversity we have all the more reason to be content, because we know that in rejoicing we give pleasure to our Lord. What greater consolation can we seek when it is to please our Jesus?”

- “Always cheerful, for so God wants!”

- “Trust in God and you will have everything; be cheerful with Jesus: yes, my little daughter, when we have the eternal God with us, what more do we lack? Nothing, nothing!”

Wednesday

Tr. pp. 67-68, “If Jesus Christ is the Son… on the bare cross”

If Jesus Christ is the Son of God and as man the Son of Mary, Our Lady is not only mother of the Church but symbolizes her most splendid icon, the living image of the very mission of the Church. She was the first to believe that the Messiah would be “Son of God,” by the explicit revelation made to her by the archangel Gabriel: “The one to be born of you will be great and will be called Son of the Most High… and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32).

The dramatic dialogue before the Sanhedrin and Mary’s very wonder at the angel’s greeting pose a serious problem: the people of the old Covenant were certain that the Messiah would come. But did they know that the Messiah would be the Son of God? He would be a great king, a liberator, a redeemer, but would he be God himself incarnate in the person of the Word?

The fact is of a divinely exceptional greatness, so that when Peter declares: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” Jesus answers him: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (cf. Matt 16:16-17).

With the mystery of the incarnation of the Word, who is God, the promises made to Abraham, to the Patriarchs, to Moses, to the Prophets take on extraordinary dimensions, above every poor human imagination. Even the prophecy that the Messiah would be Emmanuel could be understood in different ways. What the omnipotence of God could have accomplished, only the facts and Jesus’ own open confession have revealed to us, putting us in possession of this reality superior to all human imagination. For this reason the basic virtue of faith in the divinity of Christ is necessary above all.

Then faith becomes unconditional adherence to Jesus Christ, the Word incarnate: born in poverty and dead, naked, on the bare cross.

Thursday

D. pp. 76-78, par. 4

The enemy’s challenge does not weaken her fidelity to the Father’s will and her one longing to be like Jesus and in Jesus. In her words one feels all the strength that the witness of the Beloved’s life brings her: “…
