Obedient to death, even death on a cross” (Phil 2:8); “…Jesus said: It is finished. And bowing his head, he handed over the spirit…” (John 19:30).

If Jesus died for the life of the Church and of the world, she too is ready to die for the life of the Work of God:

“All of a sudden I feel someone approaching. Oh! it was my Good Jesus, my Beloved! I felt myself pressed to him and remained thus absorbed in my Good. I saw a man holding a stylus in his hand, in the act of wanting to plunge it into my throat… with an angry voice he said to me: ‘withdraw from this work or I will kill you’…”

“It will never be. Even if I had to undergo all the martyrdoms of this earth I will always be your slave and you my Beloved.

A Voice answered me: look at me, how gentle I am, and a little lamb appeared to me. It had the wound in its breast, which poured blood: what an impression this sight made on me! It caressed me, its approach made me die of love. The fire on the side of the heart was very strong and lasted quite a while, alas. My Love, I am dying. Oh my dear little Lamb!” (M. 1.1, pp. 147-148).

United with her Beloved, she frequently lives the obligatory passage of trial, but those of the absence of the Beloved are atrocious.

When the Beloved is present, even if not yet in fullness as in glory, paradise is in her; but she must pass through the painful experience of him, who lived to an infinite degree this void between presence and absence, with that density which those who reject the divine presence are destined to live.

This void, willed and not removed, is the permanent sorrow of the Beloved and she must taste it in order to offer herself in the name of those who inflict it on him, so that they may come to an adequate knowledge of the reality of God and of man.

The personal, profound experience of what the Beloved makes her live transforms her too, who becomes the Beloved. Only thus can he ask her to join in his redemptive offering for the salvation of sinners:

“Jesus said to me thus: ‘See, my beloved, when you rejected me and fled from my sight, so the cloud in which I was, and I called you many times and you always turned elsewhere and drove me away, and I abandoned you, you sought me, but no longer found me. So it is with the damned, they will no longer find me!’ Oh! what pains, yes my Good, it is a cruel torment that I felt. Oh! the mere thought of it makes me shudder…” (M. 1.1, p. 168).

This infused knowledge motivates, beyond every human criterion, her absolute offering for the salvation of sinners.

Friday

D. pp. 71-72, par. 1

The same Jesus whom the Gospels present beside Martha and Mary in tears, in the act of supporting the widow of Nain and of absolving the sinful woman, while he weeps over Jerusalem for her children, we find, in the experience described, at Rosa’s side:

“But when they (the tribulations) reached a degree at which I felt myself failing, behold, my Good took everything away from me and I remained in perfect calm.

I had my Beloved near. Oh! what I felt!

Although I no longer saw him because he had gone, still I would never have ceased to remain like one who prays, does not pray, I should say, who is savoring what her Beloved has given her…” (M. 1.1, p. 10).

In this savoring and contemplating of what Jesus gives her in love, she comes to identify with him who died so that she might no longer live for herself, but for him who died and rose (cf. 2 Cor 5:14f). She experiences, like Saint Paul, that it is not she who lives, but her Beloved lives in her:

“But, it is not I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me…” (M. 1.1, p. 12).

The call to be configured to Christ Crucified demands of her the price of absolute docility to the will of the Beloved. It entails the radicalness of self-giving according to the measure of the Beloved’s own gift. He, however, supplies her with strength and perseverance in the far from easy process of identification with him:

“…Temptations came upon me and the enemy assailed me with new assaults. Such is the struggle that I remain without strength, but my Beloved arms me with his strength to resist” (M. 1.1, pp. 12-15).

“But I am weak, O my Love, give me a little of your strength to be able to resist everything; these words ended, behold, I remained in perfect calm without pain, as if restored and healed!” (M. 1.1, p. 15).

Saturday

Tr. p. 99-100, par. 2.3

The source of prayer is Jesus Christ, the Word incarnate, his Word and his example.

The teacher of prayer is the Church with her liturgy, which has us retrace and meditate on the individual mysteries of the life of Jesus. The Church also helps us to pray with the liturgical prayers of the Mass.

Prayer is the weapon that advances the Kingdom of God in us and in the Church herself, as Mother Rosa attests:

“My Love, make use once of this miserable instrument to revive the faith and the conversion of sinners” (M. 1,1, p. 60).

It is a gift of God because, by virtue of sharing in the divine life, which is grace, it makes us sharers in the value and efficacy of Jesus’ own prayer.

For this reason the human person, when praying, accomplishes the greatest work possible to a creature. Vital union with Jesus “I am the vine, you are the branches” is therefore of a universal beneficial efficacy.

Our prayer, sharing in the sacrifice and prayer of Christ, acquires the dimensions of his own prayer.

For this reason even a simple ejaculatory prayer, uttered with faith and hope, is something immensely great, so that it is never right to say: “my prayer is worth little.” It would be worth little if it lacked the foundation of faith and were detached from the prayer of Jesus Christ, but when the soul is in grace, it is impossible for its prayer to be a small thing.

5th Sunday of Easter

D. pp. 125-126, “In the Church to proclaim… is confirmed in Rome”

Through the contemplation of the divine mysteries and listening to the Voice, which in her interior formulates a precise desire of the Father: “INCREASE OF FAITH,” Rosa experiences the dynamism that the Spirit impresses on the Church and on each of her members so that the purpose for which the world was created may be fulfilled. The Father, in fact, created it in view of the Church and of communion with his divine life, a communion realized through the proclamation and acceptance of salvation. As Jesus began his Church by preaching the Good News, the coming of the Kingdom of God promised for centuries in the Scriptures, so Rosa, keeping alive the words suggested to her in secret: “Increase of Faith,” gathers her strength to give herself to the cause of her Good.

A living member of the Church, “a branch united to the vine,” she sacrifices herself with love and for love to the Father’s plan. The support for making the gift of herself to her God Rosa finds in the Church.

Jesus endowed his Church with a structure: the authority of Peter with the other Apostles, which will remain until the full accomplishment of the Kingdom.

The Apostles, in fact, share in the mission of Jesus, in his power, but also in his fate. Through the authority of the successors of Peter and of the Apostles, the Word of the Father, even if at times not easy to understand and accept, is confirmed to Rosa.

Monday

D. pp. 83-84, “Walk in my presence… this pain that I suffer”

“Walk In My Presence…

The Voice again with its usual sweetness: try it, it is my desire, and then I said, no, this Voice is my Good because I know it too well, and the ugly one who speaks to me secretly is the dragon. And at once I set to it, indeed I made those irons myself and then put them on. They had on a skin most atrocious points and I felt nothing, not even that night, they were sweetest pains. Oh! sweet Love, what did I receive as a gift? Oh! sweetness (rapt in Him I enjoyed the most beautiful and dear delights, illuminations) he taught me so many beautiful things” (M. 1.1, p. 138).

Adherence to God, through love, opens the soul to receive a new light. In the new horizon she sees clearly the holiness of God and everything in her and in others that is out of harmony.

From this light is born a new tension that causes a suffering all the greater in that it makes the soul perceive the intensity of its natural attachments.

Here is how Rosa describes this interior dynamism, the light that enlightens her and the witness of mercy of her Good:

“To suffer and to rejoice. Oh! how useful these lights are to me, in a flash I see everything. Oh! what I feel, how I feel myself all a flame and I set about correcting that defect with such force because it is an offense to my Good. Be silent, heartless ones, why do you offend my dear Crucified One? What has he done to you that you (offend him) so barbarously? I feel so much sorrow, but Jesus is silent. Through the depths of his immense mercy, he suffers and does not punish. Oh! my Love, so many times I beg him to take from me this pain that I suffer” (M. 1.1, p. 140).

Tuesday

D. pp. 130-131, par. 4

So that Rosa may carry out her mission, the Holy Spirit provides her with various charismatic gifts. Endowed with the divine gifts and faithful to the Spirit’s inspirations, she receives the strength to proclaim and intensify the Kingdom of God among different peoples.”

It is a mission to be carried out with a portion of the Church (daughters and sons) that she receives as a gift from her Savior. The whole Church, in fact, was born of the total gift of Christ, anticipated in the Eucharist and accomplished on the cross. Jesus grants her the perception of how he is the Lord of the Church and above all of how he loves infinitely and nourishes every part and member of it:

“…having received Holy Communion my Savior appeared to me and let me see his heart: it was so great that I cannot describe it, and with his arm, resting on it, he held up a great thing that I cannot describe. He said to me: this is my Work, this Institute is my work, and he held it close. He told me so many things and also that he accepted my suffering…” (M. 12.2, p. 53f).

Suffering and love mark the development of the work entrusted to her, just as they marked the Work of Christ.

The Church, therefore, will not have her fulfillment except in the glory of heaven, at the moment of Christ’s glorious return; until that day she continues her pilgrimage amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God. Here below she feels herself in exile, far from the Lord. The fulfillment of the Church in glory will come about through many trials. Then all the just will be united in the universal Church.

Wednesday

FS p. 205, “Jesus Christ the Beloved… in her letters”

Jesus Christ, the Beloved.

From what has been said so far, one could almost speak of a certain theocentrism in the spirituality of Rosa Gattorno. In reality, however, her piety, which is faith and love, opens with all its impetus to the Incarnate God, her beloved Spouse, her Beloved, as she likes to call him. In the affectionate meditations of Lent 1864 we have a testimony of the intensity of her love for Jesus, specifically for the suffering Jesus (M 2, pp. 77-187). But on every page of her Memoirs, in every letter of hers, Jesus appears as the object of her love, the center of her life.

“When one has Jesus, one has the whole world.”

- “To grow in the spirit and love of Jesus”: this is the ideal of every daughter of St. Anne (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 12/16/1868, 10/1/1869; Circ. 1886). She would have wanted all of them enamored, mad for sweet Jesus.

“If you knew how much Jesus loves you — she wrote to a postulant — surely, mad, you would be his and would do nothing else than press him to your heart and say to him: Speak to me, command me!” (Letter to Caterina Rapallino: 1868).

“To live for Jesus,” “to see Jesus in everything,” are frequent recommendations in her letters.

Thursday

FS pp. 217-219, “The treasure of the Eucharistic presence… Blessed Sacrament”

The treasure of the Eucharistic presence.

The “great mystery of our faith” had become the continual object of her adoration and her love. She remained absorbed before this “one and immense treasure of our soul” (Letter to Emilia di Fitalia: 9/4/1889). Very often this faith was transformed into experience through vision, especially when in adoration with the Blessed Sacrament exposed; but also when she contemplated it enclosed in the tabernacle. She prayed thus one day in 1866:

“Satisfy me, for pity’s sake, with your love! Oh! why do I not remain forever before your ciborium where, my Beloved, you are enclosed? What are five, six hours a day? A nothing! Let me remain near you without moving any more… Light of my eyes, sweet Love of mine! If men knew you, surely they would leave everything and come to the feet of your altar to enjoy your delights. But how can I make them understand?…” (M 1.1, p. 43f).

She was happy when, on her visit to Pius IX, in January 1866, she obtained from the Pontiff an autograph granting her the faculty of keeping the Blessed Sacrament in the house (FIOCCHI, I, p. 109). In Piacenza she wanted her little cell next to the chapel; so, even during the night, she directed to Jesus in the sacrament her acts of adoration and her affections through the little window opened in the wall.

She often speaks of the long stretches of time she spent absorbed in close union with him, sometimes even the whole night (M 3, p. 79; 4.1, pp. 12f, 18; 4.4, pp. 26f, 95f, 114f).

One of the forms of her piety, always original, was to transport herself in spirit to the chapels of the various houses of the Institute to join her spiritual daughters in the homage of love to the Lord present in the tabernacle (M 4.1, p. 87f).

She taught them to turn to him in difficult moments:

“If you find yourself sad, run to church and cry out, weep with Jesus, and then, having dried your tears, behold, back to work, all to all and full of sweet unction to give to others” (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 5/13/1872).

Eucharistic adoration, though not prescribed by the Rule, became customary in the houses of the Daughters of St. Anne with a sufficient number of sisters, above all in the Mother House. But because of their mission in service of the Church they could not give themselves full time to such an act of worship; so Mother Rosa welcomed with joy the offer by the bishop of Piacenza, Bishop Scalabrini, of the direction of an institute for deaf-mute girls that he had opened in 1880. The interest she felt for those creatures, being the mother of a deaf-mute daughter, came to join her desire to see Jesus adored in the Eucharist. On December 8, 1884, with the clothing of the first five deaf-mute girls, the community of the Tertiaries of St. Anne, Perpetual Adorers of the Blessed Sacrament, began.

Friday

D. pp. 110-111, “The Spirit and the mission… whatever is asked of me”

The Holy Spirit, whom the Father reveals through his mission in time: in creation, in the word of the Prophets, in the Incarnation of the Word in the womb of Mary, in the life of the Son and in his work, in the proclamation and work of the Apostles after the glorification of Jesus, fully manifests the fullness of the Trinitarian mystery and continues his work in the mission of the Church.

His mission unfolds from then on in the children adopted by the Father in Christ Jesus.”

The life and mission of Rosa, as daughter in the Son, are therefore a mystical place of the Presence and mission of the Spirit.

Her “time” - the slice of history entrusted by the Father to her - was a time of the Spirit and of witness, but also a time marked by various needs and by trials that did not spare her, a time of vigilance and confident waiting. On every page of her Memoirs the presence of the Spirit in her life and mission is attested:

“…but He, who governs and works in this very work of his, knows very well how to take away and give as he pleases… the mental illuminations became much clearer and livelier, so that, to my astonishment, I feel such sublime words come out of my mouth, and I find everything easy: to preach, to expound and to resolve whatever is asked of me…” (M. 3, P-1).

Saturday

FS pp. 22-23, “A strong and courageous spirit… rest for an eternity!”

A strong and courageous spirit.

A woman of character is defined by those who knew her. The Benedictine Don Domenico Serafini, who for two years, during Mother Rosa’s lifetime, was apostolic visitor of the Daughters of St. Anne, describes her as “a woman of piety, of an uncommon mind and of great energy.”

In the critical moments of her life she showed herself in command of herself, resolute and courageous. So, for example, in the family events, as wife and as widow; in the alternative of leaving her own children and parents to consecrate herself to the interests of God; in the attitude she took toward the persons and situations, some harsh and humiliating, that she had to face as foundress.

Sick from the very beginning of her widowhood, weakened by fasting, vigils, and other penances, subject moreover to the pain of the hidden stigmata and to the burnings of the heart, which produced frequent fainting spells, she worked tirelessly in her office, undertook long and wearisome journeys, visited the houses of the Institute listening to all the sisters, dealt with prelates and benefactors…; and she managed to master her own weakness and weariness, so as to appear, as they say, always in form.

And she knew how to instill courage in her collaborators, in the superiors, in individual sisters and in other persons who confided in her. Hardly is there a letter of hers in which the word does not leap out: Courage! Here are some of the words of encouragement we find in her letters to the sisters, amid vibrant expressions of affection:

“My dear child, come, courage!” - “Be of good heart, for heaven is favorable to you!” - “Courage, my dear! let us work, for then we shall rest blessed. Be strong, do not fear!” - “Patience, my dear, courage!… courage!” - “My beloved ones, courage, for one day you will see your God and will enjoy your labors” - “Courage, and all trust in the good God!” - “Courage, for in the moment of trial one needs courage and patience, peace and resignation. With this everything is obtained and every obstacle overcome” - “Courage! If the road is closed on all sides, one must go forward by dint of sweat of blood, as long as we have one drop in our veins!” - “First commend yourself to God, and then forward with courage!” - “Courage, my daughter! for one day we shall taste the fruit of the blood and sweat shed in our labors!” - “Courage, forward! for one day we shall be at rest for an eternity!”

6th Sunday of Easter

FS pp. 150-152, Carrying the cross… of his most beloved brides”

The suffering of the Christian, according to Jesus’ invitation (Matt 10:38; Luke 9:23; 14:27) and the theology of Saint Paul (Gal 2:19; 6:14), has a name: the Cross. And it is the name preferred by Mother Rosa. She confesses that even in 1859, enticed by the great consolations of those beginnings, she was not accustomed to “fighting under the banner of the holy Cross, delightful and dear.” She was a “beginner” (M 1.1, p. 4). But she was not long in entering fully into the school of the Cross: it will always be her “companion,” her “bed of rest” (M 3, p. 25). One day when she was full of bitterness, holding the cross tightly, she spoke thus with it: “Is it true, my treasure, that you are always my companion?” And she heard a voice that comforted her: “Only from the Cross does one learn to love!” (TC, p. 329).

Not content with constantly having the image of the Crucified before the eyes of body and spirit, she wanted to make her love tangible by tying a small cross tightly to her breast, taking her brief rest lying on a cross and often remaining hanging on a large wooden cross that she had in her little room in Piacenza. But it was the very mystery of the Cross, more than its materiality, that had configured her life.

And she would have wanted each of the daughters of St. Anne to become a true lover of the Cross. Encouragements in this sense are very frequent in her letters; here are some:

“Courage on the way of Calvary, if you want to come to be crucified with your Beloved and die with him on the delightful bed of the Cross”

- “Every new day, a new cross! Blessed is the one whose dawn breaks amid thorns and pains!”

- “In paradise there is no more cross, there there are no more sufferings: only Love, Love… Cheerful, cheerful, for Jesus likes those who suffer: whoever does not want to suffer does not want to love!”

- “Whoever wants to follow me — says the Master showing us a cross — let him take up his cross and follow me. So, what language is this, heavenly Spouse? O blessed souls! He gives me that treasure which the world does not know and which he offers to his beloved brides, and even seeks that it be heavy, so that one day they may come to taste his delights”

- “This holy Wood, nuptial bed of his most beloved brides!” (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 5/27/1869, 1/1/1870; to Sr. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1869, 1/16/1870; to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: 12/23/1868, 2/6/1870).

Monday

D. pp. 101-102, “The description Rosa gives of her experience… rich testimony”

The description Rosa gives of her experience with the Spirit allows us to grasp this discreet presence in the movement that goes from the contemplation of the Face of Christ to the mysterious experience of the fire that devours and consumes her:

“…I saw the face of my Redeemer. Oh! how beautiful it was! What joy, my love! It was so luminous that I would not know how to explain its light and beauty. I felt wholly inflamed by that object which consumed me. Ah! when will be that day when in so beautiful a moment you, O my Good, will consume me?” (M. 1.1, p. 13).

The Spirit draws her to Jesus: he awakens in her like a devouring fire, but what in turn arouses this power of love is the sight of the Redeemer.

The Spirit, in fact, shows her in the most splendid light the Face of her Redeemer, makes her fall in love with irresistible attraction and with a strength that is no longer her own. He, though present, is overshadowed by Rosa’s act of love for her Redeemer. He is like a mother who gives birth to her own child by giving herself so that he may live.

She therefore knows him in relation to Christ, through the light that illumines his face and the fire that Christ’s very presence kindles in her. The experience of the Presence of the Spirit as Love points to his Identity: the Third divine Person of the Trinity is Love, the essence of God himself: “God is Love…; in this we know that we remain in him and he in us: he has given us of his Spirit,” “whoever remains in love remains in God and God in him” (1 John 4:8; 13; 16).

The Scriptures, in reference to the reality “Spirit-Love”: “The love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us” (Rom 5:5), offer a rich testimony.

Tuesday

D. pp. 99-100, par. 1

The Holy Spirit, as he prepared Mary throughout the history of salvation and worked continually in her with grace, continues to act in every person. With the same grace he awakens faith and gives rise to new life in Rosa, giving her an exclusive taste for God and a growing love for Jesus Crucified and for her neighbor. Rosa’s writings admirably attest the work of grace in her person:

“…having been left free of every bond I devoted myself with more fervor to pious works and to visiting the hospitals, the poor sick at home, helping them in everything.

By the grace of the Lord I noticed that all earthly affections were dissipating, nothing was any longer tasty to me, only my God was the pasture of all my delights. The sorrows… I poured into the heart of my Dear Crucified One, for him alone, I kept repeating to myself, all my suffering is little because I had committed many sins…” (M. 1.1, p. 1).

Moved by the grace of the Holy Spirit, she feels drawn to her dear Crucified One, unified in her affections to the point of concentrating all her desires and tastes in God, purified, transformed, and urged to grow in love. The life of the Spirit nourishes her, heals her, organizes her activities, sends her to serve those who suffer and to bear witness to the gift she has received.

The one who works in her, comes to meet her weakness, forgives her sins and intercedes for her needs is the Spirit (cf. Rom 8:26). (2).

Wednesday

D. pp. 105-107, “The Holy Spirit perfects… Yes, my Love”

The Holy Spirit perfects Rosa’s faith. The very One who works from creation: “…the Spirit of God hovered over the waters” (Gen 1:2) and who spoke through the Prophets, dwells in Rosa’s interior to teach her everything as Jesus promised: “…the Holy Spirit whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of all that I told you” (John 14:26).

Approaching the writings introduces us into her interior reality flooded with the lights of the Spirit, who guides her with the Voice, with the gift of discernment (cf. M. 1.1, p. 63) and other signs in the moments of growth in holiness and in the decisive steps of the mission:

“…he always teaches me, warns me, oh, in this how severe he is. In the smallest things he warns me where I fall short and he does not like it that I do not do such and such a thing at once…”;

“Oh, how many beautiful lessons he gave me. He explained certain doubts of mine, he let me see what I had to go through…” (M. 1.1, pp. 109; 144).

Christ, the Beloved, in the Spirit opens her mind for the exercise of discernment in action and enlightens her about the essence and degrees of love:

“I was instructed about a certain thing to be done. He instructed me about his love, its degree and how it is communicated to the soul… I saw everything immense, great without equal. I saw how the soul, to receive this Love, must be well purified; thus one feels that one burns, is consumed, but the ardent longing grows, the ardent longing to consume and burn all the more. Oh, incomprehensible mystery: To suffer and to enjoy infinitely the delights of the Beloved! One always desires only him and for him everything is little. Yes, my Love” (M. 1.2, p. 45).

Thursday

Tr. p. 152, “The Church is holy… eternal life”

The Church is holy because her members are baptized, and Saint Paul calls the baptized “saints” (cf. Titus 3:5; Eph 5:26; 1 Cor 6:11).

Upon them, thanks to baptism, the Spirit of the Father and of the Son is reflected.

The Council devotes Chapter II of Lumen Gentium to the Church as “people of God.”

“Christ the Lord, High Priest taken from among men (cf. Heb 5:1-5), made the new people ‘a kingdom of priests to God, his Father’ (Rev 1:6; cf. 5:9-10). By regeneration and the anointing of the Holy Spirit the baptized are consecrated to be a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, in order to offer, through all the works of the Christian, spiritual sacrifices, and to proclaim the marvels of him who called them out of darkness into his wonderful light (cf. 1 Pet 2:4-10). All the disciples of Christ, therefore, persevering in prayer and praising God together (cf. Acts 2:42-47), should present themselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God (cf. Rom 12:1), bear witness to Christ everywhere and, to those who ask, give an account of the hope of eternal life that is in them (cf. 1 Pet 3:15)” (LG 10).

Friday

FS pp. 180-181, “Setbacks, misunderstandings… such situations”

Setbacks, misunderstandings, and persecutions are the normal patrimony of all who commit themselves to following Christ. The life of Rosa Gattorno could not be an exception. From the time she accepted, by God’s will, her mission as foundress, she understood that it is the mark of every evangelical undertaking to have to face, first of all, the postulates of human prudence and then the opposition, not only of the enemies of the interests of the Kingdom, but also of the good and well-intentioned who do not share or understand the viewpoints of one who acts under the divine impulse.

She was conscious of being an instrument of God, though an unskilled one: her foundation was the Work of God. It is no wonder that in every opponent she saw an adversary of God’s plan, even an unwitting collaborator of the evil one. Hence her deep suffering, especially when she discovered in her opponents hypocrisy, ulterior motives, and hidden personal interests. Nor let us forget her tendency to turn every unforeseen event into a motive and opportunity for suffering. In reality she had to endure real slanders, all the more painful as they came from persons to whom she had given trust, affection, and sacrifice (cf. FIOCCHI, I, pp. 181f, 186-189, 199-220); or from those whom she deeply venerated as ministers of the Church.

It is not the place to list the many occasions that embittered and purified her spirit, already so tried by interior pains. We will limit ourselves to hinting at her feelings in the face of such situations.

Saturday

Tr. pp. 130-131, par. 3.2

Choosing Mary Immaculate as their model, they become a sign of hope for the person of today in the preferential action for the poorest, knowing how to identify and relieve the new poverties. They therefore work for integral liberation in the sense of that freedom with which Christ has set us free (as Saint Paul warns). Christ has set us free so that we might remain free: “Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery” (Gal 5:1).

This is the great freedom that sprang from the redemptive death of Christ. An immensely deep freedom that ransoms man from the slavery of Satan and of sin, not in the restricted sense of mere “political” freedom to which the freedom of Christ is sometimes reduced, but in the sense of integral freedom, a prophetic sign of hope for the person of today.

7th Sunday of Easter (or Ascension)

D. pp. 129-130, par. 3

Union with Christ is for every baptized person nuptiality and mission. It becomes the sacrament of the unity of the human race with its Creator and Father.

The unity already begun with the Paschal mystery of Christ must be prolonged through the Church and every member of the Church. The disciple of Christ must project himself into the world so that “people of every nation, race, people, and language” may be gathered around him: “And Jesus came and said to them: - All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age…” (Matt 28:18-20).

As the Church, in the hands of Christ, is an instrument of redemption for all, the universal sacrament of salvation, so Rosa, being a living member of the Church - in this sense the whole life and mission of the Church is in her, and her personal life and mission is in the life of the Church - unveils by proclaiming and at the same time accomplishes the mystery of God’s love for man.

On the horizon of the words of Jesus, addressed to all disciples of every age, there emerge those spoken for her alone while she is absorbed by the presence of the Crucified One:

“They will devote themselves to the increase of our holy faith; to the assistance of the sick…; they will receive… in their care girls in danger and will teach Christian doctrine…”

Monday

Tr. pp. 68-69, “With the mystery of the Incarnation… increase our faith”

With the mystery of the incarnation of the Word, who is God, the promises made to Abraham, to the Patriarchs, to Moses, to the Prophets take on extraordinary dimensions, above every poor human imagination. Even the prophecy that the Messiah would be Emmanuel could be understood in different ways. What the omnipotence of God could have accomplished, only the facts and Jesus’ own open confession have revealed to us, putting us in possession of this reality superior to all human imagination. For this reason the basic virtue of faith in the divinity of Christ is necessary above all.

Then faith becomes unconditional adherence to Jesus Christ, the Word incarnate: born in poverty and dead, naked, on the bare cross.

Such truth necessarily leads to total adherence to the supreme mystery of the most holy Trinity, the threefold ocean of infinite love into which the Word inserts us while we are still pilgrims on earth. For souls straining toward perfection and arrived at the highest summits, like Mother Rosa, immersed continually in this adherence, it becomes total trust, interior, familiar, and uninterrupted dialogue. The virtue of faith in God can and must grow day by day. For this reason we must make our own the prayer the Apostles addressed to Jesus: “We believe, Lord, increase our faith!” (Luke 17:5).

Tuesday

D. pp. 108-109, par. 4

The Spirit Paraclete (the One called alongside), sent by Jesus to all people to move them to love with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the strength, who also came to convict the “world in regard to sin” (John 16:8), is Rosa’s interior teacher.

She specifies, in her Memoirs, that the Spirit guides her, enlightens her, and purifies her on the path of sanctification:

“Oh, my Love! I was rapt in him: what I saw, what I felt…! He let me see certain imperfections; although I know that I am a heap of infamies, yet in that union, my Good washes my poor soul which remains purified in the fire of his divine Love. Oh! sweetness!…” (M. 1.2, p. 118).

On another page, describing union with her God, she adds:

“…I remained so convinced of my nothingness… that it seemed to me I no longer had the courage to be in the presence of my God…, the more intimate the union became, the more I discovered my nothingness…”;

“…I was afflicted because I had no one to say a word to. A Voice said to me: ‘why do you say this? do you not remember what I told you a short time before such a defeat reached you from Rome? I am your Master, be calm. The peace of conscience that I enjoy in the midst of so many tribulations… is such that I see there is a most powerful Spirit who sustains me…’” (M. 3, p. 21; M. 4.1, p. 4).

Rosa is conformed to Christ by this Presence dwelling in her, who animates her, sustains her, goes before her and accompanies her in the fulfillment of her vocation to holiness.

Wednesday

Tr. pp. 140-142, par. 1.3

Holiness is the goal of creation and of redemption. “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev 11:44; 11:45; 19:2; 20:7; 20:26; 21:8) God had already said to the chosen people of the old Covenant, and one can say that all of God’s interventions, directly or indirectly through the Prophets, are a call to holiness.

The universal call to holiness is therefore not a novelty of recent centuries. It is a divine imperative impressed on human nature itself from creation, which has holiness as its goal, in the same way as redemption.

In both the three divine persons are engaged: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. To the Father is particularly attributed the concept of principle, principle of every principle and of every reality and therefore also of creation; to the Son redemption; to the Holy Spirit sanctification.

This distinction of functions is theologically logical. If holiness consists in the perfection of charity, as the Second Vatican Council expresses it, the Holy Spirit is charity itself, the third Person of the most holy Trinity.

The Father created us; the Son redeemed us and made us children of God; the Holy Spirit sanctifies us with an action always in act. His presence, silent and discreet, is recognized by the dynamism of love that he arouses (cf. The Gift of God…, pp. 101ff.).

Mother Rosa’s experience attests the manifold operations of the Holy Spirit and urges us to adhere with love to each divine person so as to become docile, like her, to their initiative: “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (cf. Rom 8:14); “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (cf. 1 Cor 3:16).

Let us make our own, contemplating them, all the attributes that he let Mother Rosa experience: sanctifying grace, creative activity, fire of love, light that illumines minds and conscience, physician of souls, spiritual guide, tireless worker, voice that orients and directs in the work of the Father and in that of Jesus, interior strength, sweet consoler.

Let us also repeat often the prayers to the Holy Spirit, as the Church, teacher of prayer, invokes him in the Liturgy of the Holy Spirit: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love.”

And with his coming we shall experience that his action is the active, operative presence of God’s mercy in the soul, tied to the merits of Jesus the Redeemer in accordance with what the New Testament reveals to us.

Thursday

Tr. pp. 142-144, par. 1.4

The person docile to the action of grace reaches the full maturity of Christ as son in the Son.

Docility to the action of the Spirit makes of us new creatures, transformed into the image of Christ Jesus and ever more conscious of living in him, through him and with him the inheritance that he acquired for us by offering himself as victim of the new Covenant.

The Father himself illumines this reality of ours through his Word: “The Holy Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs, heirs of God, joint heirs with Christ, if only we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him. I consider that the sufferings of this present time are as nothing compared with the glory to be revealed for us” (Rom 8:16-18).

Having, then, to share in the suffering of Christ, and the Father knowing our weakness, he does not leave us alone in the effort of identification with the firstborn Son of every person.

“The Spirit comes to the aid of our weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes with inexpressible groanings. And the one who searches hearts knows what is the desire of the Spirit, because he intercedes for the holy ones according to God’s will. We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those he predestined he also glorified” (Rom 8:28-30).

Mother Rosa firmly believed in God’s plan, and so did not spare her life, always hoping, even against all hope, in him, her Good, her fortress, and her defender: “Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who acquits. Who will condemn? It is Christ Jesus who died, rather, was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed intercedes for us. What will separate us from the love of Christ? Will anguish, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?

As it is written: for your sake we are being put to death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.

But in all these things we conquer overwhelmingly through him who loved us.”

This same certainty must grow in us so that we may experience in life, in total surrender to the Father, how “neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor present things, nor future things, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom 8:38-39).

To be children in the Son is our destiny, but it is still the object of our hope. “In hope we were saved. Now hope that sees is not hope. For who hopes for what one sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with perseverance” (Rom 8:24-25).

Friday

Tr. pp. 78-79, “The whole history… mystical writings”

The whole history of the old and the new Covenant is centered on the divine person of Jesus, Son of God and Son of man, that is, son of the Virgin Mary, the Immaculate One.

At the foundation of the history of salvation there is therefore God’s love for the human person.

Creation and redemption are therefore realities that can be traced back to the love God has for the human creature, the first origin of all history, which finds in the incarnate Word its deepest meaning and its root.

In him and through him everything is explained and everything finds its reason and its one meeting point. One then understands well the meaning of the words in the great prayer of Jesus: “Holy Father, keep in unity those whom you have given me, that they also may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you… so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given to them, so that they may be one as we are one” (John 17:20-21). Here is the way of Christian perfection and holiness: to become one with Jesus, to identify progressively with him, to become one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The way to attain such unity was lived and taught by Mother Rosa, eager to become one with Christ crucified.

To bring hope to fulfillment is then to set it in the love of the Crucified One. From this derives the living and perennial relevance of Mother Rosa’s charism, who could well say with Saint Paul: “I resolved to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor 2:2).

This was also Mother Rosa’s wisdom (especially mystical). But this wisdom is nothing other than ardent love for Jesus and particularly for Jesus crucified, as one can easily deduce from the data of her life and from her mystical writings.

Saturday

Tr. pp. 128-130, par. 3.1

The daughters of St. Anne, and the other members of the Family, in awaiting the Lord who comes, build the kingdom in poverty of heart and maternal and paternal self-giving.

Working in the Church according to a specific mission, they cooperate in the saving work of Christ, carrying in their hearts a single passion: the Kingdom of God and the glory of the Father, following the example of the foundress.

They therefore work for the increase of holy faith, the conversion of sinners, and service to their brothers and sisters, made a sign and instrument of the Father’s merciful love for all people. Inserted in the reality of the local church, they are a ferment of communion, witnesses of hope and a presence of proclamation, and they build the kingdom in poverty of heart and maternal and paternal self-giving.

As St. Anne awaited the fulfillment of the promises, the one sent by the Father, so they too, while they hope for the glorious manifestation of the Lord, burning with zeal like Mother Rosa, strive to make him known to the whole world in the certainty that God has worked, works, and will continue to work great things in persons through prayer and our active apostolic work, even when the cross of Jesus, physical or spiritual, invites us to walk, at least in part, the way of Calvary.

It is the cross and the Crucified One that Mother Rosa loved with so much ardor and generous devotion, just as the Psalm says: “Lord, my rock and my fortress, my deliverer, my God, my rock of refuge, my shield, my saving horn, my stronghold. The breakers of death surged round about me, the floods of perdition overwhelmed me; the snares of death were before me. In my distress I called upon the Lord, to my God I cried out; from his temple he heard my voice, my cry to him reached his ears” (Ps 18:3.7).

In these words of the Psalm the great sufferings, mystical as well, of the Mother foundress are well foreshadowed, she who knew how to unite hope and love, joy and sorrow, “rejoicing like a champion to run its course” (Ps 19:6).

She knew how to walk the way of holiness and of the apostolate, in the footsteps of Christ suffering and crucified, almost repeating with Jesus: “There is a baptism with which I must be baptized - the baptism of blood - and how great is my anguish until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50). And those words spoken on the eve of the passion: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15).

Pentecost

Tr. p. 144-147, par. 1.5

Holiness, the work of “divine Love” that strengthens, sustains, frees, transforms, shapes

The Holy Spirit nourishes in us the hope of being freed from slavery to corruption and from the fear of sin “to enter into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom 8:21).

Yes, the Holy Spirit guides us to freedom, to the whole truth, to holiness. The whole truth is Jesus: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” The Holy Spirit, who works without rest, continues his descent into souls: on the day of Pentecost upon Mary most holy and the apostles in a perceptible and thunderous way; from then on in a gentle and silent way, to impress on those who thirst for the love of God and for holiness the seal of the seven gifts: Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Piety, Fear of the Lord, understood as fear of offending his love, fear of not responding generously to his aspirations.

The Holy Spirit continues always to work in persons, producing in them his fruits: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law” (Gal 5:22-23).

Pentecost, therefore, is not over, it continues in souls where it finds the assurance of hope, the insatiable thirst for perfection, the earnest will to grow in that charity of which Saint Paul speaks (cf. 1 Cor 13:1ff.). At this point one would say that everything on the way of holiness is the work of the Holy Spirit.

But everything is also the work of the Father: We have not received a spirit of slavish fear, but the spirit of adoption of children, in which we cry out: Abba, Father! The Holy Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (cf. Rom 8:15).

Therefore everything is also owed to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. From his divine fatherhood every “earthly human fatherhood and motherhood takes its origin and meaning” (Eph 3:15).

Not for nothing does Jesus speak continually of the Father, to such a point that one day the Apostle Philip says to him: “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.” And Jesus answers him: “Have I been with you for so long a time and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (cf. John 14:8-10).

Therefore everything depends on the Father, everything depends on the Holy Spirit. It is no less true, however, that everything depends on the Son: “All things came to be through him, and without him nothing came to be of what exists” (John 1:3).

In this regard let us also recall the prologue of Saint Paul to the letter to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians.

Everything has been made and everything is accomplished by the Father, by the Son, by the Holy Spirit. The Trinity of persons does not remove the unity of nature. The three divine persons are perfectly immanent, one in the other. The unity of nature does not remove the reality of the three Persons and their distinction and the distinct attributions. God thrice holy, thrice infinite love, thrice our creator and our redeemer.

This does not remove the fact that the supreme divine work is the Incarnation by which the Son took on human nature, the Word as man brought divine nature close to us, to the point of being called “God with us.” The most lovable face of the Redeemer and Savior introduces us into the ineffable great mystery of the most holy Trinity.

Before this revealed truth, how can one not be deeply moved in pronouncing the word Father! How not to be moved before the Child born in Bethlehem of the Immaculate One, how not to be moved when we sing with the Church: “Come, O Creator Spirit, come light of minds, come, O Holy Spirit,” you who are the “Gift” par excellence, Giver of all gifts.

“Come, we too implore,

Come, Holy Spirit

make of us your living temple!

Dwell

in us, pray in us, guide us to holiness,

You are the infinite love

of the Father and of the Son,

you, beatifying infinite light.”

Most Holy Trinity

D. pp. 32-33, par. 1

Access To The Trinitarian Mystery.

Intimate union with Christ and Christ Crucified has raised her to the degree of love required by him so that the Trinity may reveal itself to her.

The description Rosa has left us of the contemplation of the Trinity in 1864 places us before the inaccessible mystery of God, which she, in her human limitation, cannot express with corresponding words.

Even though the sense of God’s life in her was developed, nevertheless, before the experience that surpasses all human understanding she writes only out of obedience to her Good and lets herself be guided by him:

“Great beyond all telling is the Sacrosanct Triad, infinite in God alone, infinite in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Equal in unity, perfect in Trinity. God alone as person alone is seen, and at once in Jesus and in the Holy Spirit, in gazing at the excellence and exquisiteness of these three Persons in whom one always discerns one person and three without being divided! My Love! (M. 1.2, p. 1).

In an instant she sees and understands the Life of God the Trinity in the depth willed by him himself. A knowledge that is not given to be attained by human faculties alone. Infused knowledge, in fact, infinitely surpasses every other knowledge and even the spiritual sense of God.

In the cited vision Rosa contemplates the Most Holy Trinity in relation to itself.

Theology defines this form “Trinity in itself,” to distinguish the two ways of being, that of eternity and that of history. Infused knowledge leaves no doubts about the life of God, though the inaccessible always remains in its infinite reality.

Consciousness remains modified, shaped by the vision; the object of faith, having been experienced, has opened new horizons. As Saint Paul expresses it fourteen years after the vision of God: “I will go on to visions of the Lord. I know a man in Christ who (…) was caught up to the third heaven and heard words that no one may utter” (2 Cor 12:1-4), the experience remains, confirms faith, impresses on the affections a divine dynamism that impels the person to desire to live and remain in the reality contemplated.

The mystical event: “in everything I could say, I saw Paradise and God Triune! and then suddenly One alone, in all his beauty!” (M. 1.1, p. 58), remains, even if afterward trials supervene that cloud the transcendent horizon of the soul.

Corpus Christi

D. pp. 92-93, “The sign of the bread… Christ the heart of the world”

The sign of bread and wine opens and leads her from the vision of the mystery of the life of Christ himself to Trinitarian life and to her involvement in the paschal reality of Christ: “While I was listening to Holy Mass and offering to the Eternal Father the Sacrifice of the Altar, a most vivid light appeared to me together with a voice that said to me: this sacrifice of yourself in that Chalice together with his Beloved Son pleases God greatly, but it would please him greatly if you offered yourself as victim in all the Sacrifices that are accomplished on the altars of the whole Catholic world, and at once I did not delay in doing it; as soon as this was done I remained absorbed in God and my intellect clearly saw all the sacrifices accomplished and to be accomplished in all the Catholic Churches. I rejoiced greatly and so every morning I renew the offering: Behold, my God, your victim who unites herself to Jesus…” (M. 1.1, p. 123).

The Eucharist, Christ who becomes present in it, involves her in a radical way. The Trinity itself becomes present with interior words revealing her mission associated with that of the divine Victim, which opens her to universal horizons and directs her to the ransom of sinners.

Her unconditional response to the Father’s demands makes her grow in love; the divine fire grows in her in adoration, in apostolic and universal impetus, in faith, in understanding of the mystery the Eucharist represents: victim with the Victim in Trinitarian light, the Father’s good pleasure, offering, praise, thanksgiving, adoration that reach the universe and introduce into the hearts of sinners the echo, the call, the demand for a new humanity for a new world according to God’s plan: “to make Christ the heart of the world.”

Weeks I–XXXIV

Ordinary Time

1st Sunday of Ordinary Time

Tr. pp. 56-58, par. 3.3

The Church is truly the «people of God» to the extent that the baptized belong to Christ Jesus, to his mystical body. Precisely because the Church is identified with the «mystery hidden for ages in God», who is Jesus Christ, the reality of the Church, like that of Jesus, is the work of divine wisdom, and therefore is immensely superior to our poor human concepts and to our capacity to understand.

The Church is not only the «saved» people, the communion of believers, but also the «saving» universe.

Like Mary, the Church too begets men and women to a new and immortal life: this is her motherhood in the Holy Spirit (cf. RM 44). To suppose that the sinner as such belongs to her formally, and not virtually, leads one to think that the Church is sinful, in complete contrast with the «holy» Church. It is no accident that she is a mystery! The Church, born of the redeeming sacrifice of Christ and of the gift of the Holy Spirit, inserts us into Christ through the rite of baptism.

Baptism has always been the outward expression of faith, of insertion and of conversion, that is, of the firm decision to renounce the past, sin, radically changing one's own mentality. Only on this condition does one enter the people of God.

The image of the Church as the «people of God» must not, therefore, be isolated from the image of the Church as mystical body and immaculate bride of Christ, just as the Council in fact does not isolate it. The Church as mystical body is a phrase inspired by the Holy Spirit and so Saint Paul proclaims it, and after him the Tradition and the doctors of the Church, in particular Saint Augustine.

Only the image of the Church as mystical body allows us to understand that to separate oneself (through sin) from the Head is to separate oneself from the body, which is the members. In this sense, whoever separates from the Head separates from the members.

The image of the Church as the «people of God» has the advantage of opening the door wide also to those who do not belong to her except virtually, because all men and women, just as they have the vocation to Jesus Christ, head and king of humanity, so they have the vocation to the Church. In this sense, even those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel and the Church, but live honestly, belong to the soul and not to the body of the Church. And if they live honestly according to the natural moral law written by God in their hearts, the Lord will not fail to run to their aid and save them at the point of death. This truth, however, must not extinguish the missionary ardor kindled by Jesus on earth: «go and preach the Gospel to every creature». Who can ever calculate the advantage of those who have the grace of living united to Jesus and to his immaculate Bride, and the disadvantage of being outside her? «I have come to bring fire to the earth, and what do I want if not that this fire of truth, of love and of peace be kindled more and more?» (Lk 12:49).

It is no accident that the Church is a «mystery» and that the study of her characteristics occupies one of the most evocative treatises of Theology.

Monday

D. pp. 25-27, pars. 1 and 2

The admirable initiative of the Creator toward man reveals to us, in all vocations, in the Church and in the world, the nature of God who, in his being Love, creates, chooses, calls, unveils «man to man», and guides him from stage to stage up to the ultimate and indispensable experience of total and definitive self-giving to Him who created him by calling him into existence (cf. LG 2).

God is the One who calls and chooses whom he wills. Paul underlines this divine initiative in the letter to the Romans (9:11-13), citing the election of Jacob in preference to Esau: «When they were not yet born and had done nothing, either good or bad, God said to Rebecca: the elder shall serve the younger». This shows that God has his own plan in choosing men. His choice does not depend on their works, but on Him «who calls» (cf. Gal 5:8; 1 Pt 1:15).

God, in his free initiative, chooses man before his birth: «before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations» (Jer 1:5).

In the letter to the Galatians the apostle affirms the same truth in reference to his vocation: «But when He who set me apart from my mother's womb called me through his grace…» (Gal 1:15).

God, besides reaching man with his love by choosing him before his birth, accompanies him throughout his existence in every concrete circumstance in which he finds himself: «The Lord said to me: go to those to whom I will send you and proclaim what I command you. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to protect you» (Jer 1:7-8). He guides him to the full attainment of the fullness of life in Christ (Eph 1:3-14).

Vocation is an act of love. God calls man by «name»: «now thus says the Lord who created you…, who formed you…: Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine» (Is 43:1). The name corresponds to the unique, unrepeatable image and to the plan of life that He has conceived for each one: «I have called you by name, I have given you a title, though you do not know me» (Is 45:4).

Vocation is a constitutive reality of being. Every person is created to fulfill a mission and to be, in God's universal plan, that unique and unrepeatable identity: «The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God; and God never ceases to draw man to himself, and only in God will man find the truth and happiness he never stops searching for…». In the New Testament the Gospel of Mark presents this dynamism in the vocation of the apostles: «Jesus went up the mountain, called to himself those whom he wanted, and they came to him. He appointed twelve to be with him and also to be sent out to preach and to have authority to cast out demons» (Mk 3:13-14).

Tuesday

FS pp. 65-66, «As the invasion of the divine… were a person who

worked and lived continually in my place»

As the invasion of the divine made itself felt in her spirit, Rosa felt herself ever more purified, relieved of the impediments that hindered her impulse toward the supreme Good. Here is how she describes, in the book Travails and Comforts, the effect of those passive purifications, in a beautiful page, worthy of the great masters of mysticism:

«My Crucified subdues the humanity, gives it vigor and energy, strengthens the spirit which, victorious, rules over all the faculties, which are so well subject to it. Self-love dissipates, gets lost, so much so that even one's own name is forgotten. Pride is overcome and is looked upon as an instrument of scorn, as an enemy. One experiences great pleasures and great consolation when one sees them crushed. The will, which is overbearing, grows quiet. My Crucified has exchanged my will for his own, and it is infinitely sweet and pleasant no longer to possess it. Oh! how it would have rebelled, had He not nailed it down, while leaving it always free!» (TC, p. 3f).

With the same capacity for self-analysis, though in her own way, she describes the various ways in which she experiences the intimate presence of God and his communications: infused recollection, simple gaze of love, interior invitations, languors of love… She knows that none of this is the fruit of her own effort, but that all is pure gift of God, the experience of a life that is not her own. To express such newness she very often appropriates the well-known text of Saint Paul: It is no longer I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me (cf. Gal 2:20). She writes in 1867:

«Such was the union with my God that, as soon as I began to pray, I was at once absorbed in Him; and I always saw new things… He taught me, corrected me, showed me how I was to do his work…, as if I were not living, but within me there were a person who worked and lived continually in my place.

Wednesday

D. p. 119, par. 1

It is a distinct Voice that transcends the voice of her conscience even while respecting and shaping it. A Voice that awakens the values with which the Lord had already endowed her in creating her. A Voice that guides her path, reassures her in doubt and demands offering of her. A Voice beloved, loving, unmistakable, clearly distinguished by Rosa from the other voices that draw her away from the will of God. A Voice awaited, transforming, respectful and authoritative at once, a Voice that manifests the prerogatives of God and the aspects of the Mystery of Christ, a Voice that confirms the existence and presence of her beloved Good, of the Beloved, of the Spirit, of the Father:

«A Voice that was certainly his, my Good's, said to me: from you I want this work. Take to the Archbishop the writing you have» (M. 2, p. 11).

Thursday

D. pp. 123-124, par. 4

The tone, the style, the gentleness and firmness of the Voice train Rosa to distinguish exactly whether it comes from her God or instead from the whisperer. She becomes ever wiser «in every kind of discernment» (Phil 1:9).

«A voice that strongly said to me: now you are dead…, brought me an ugly feeling as of fright… Ah! I understand well, this is nothing but the enemy…» (M. 1.1, p. 139).

By responding docilely to the Voice she becomes God's delight. The mystical experience leads her to identify, «with all wisdom and spiritual understanding» (Col 1:9), the Voice with the will of God that is manifested to her, which is the strength of her freedom, the purpose of her life.

Faithful response to the Voice makes her joyful, grateful, steadfast in faith, persevering in hope, strong in the struggles of life and against the devil. The word spoken by the Voice takes flesh in her and in the events she manages: «It is I who live for you»; it becomes history. This Voice seeks and waits for her to speak, and the Voice lets itself be found and heard. She knows no other science than that of her Voice. She is the «humble slave of her beloved master».

Friday

Pr. Po. p. 12 «The poor man rejoices… arrogant and wicked»

The poor man rejoices in the Lord, seeks him. These poor are the descendants of the servants of God, they are a link in a long chain. It is the humble contrasted with the proud; we thus have the disposition of the two categories, which springs in turn from the two respective existential situations. One who is rich, who in life has always had everything and has never had to depend on anyone, has never undergone any constraints, will never be able to have a sense of attention to others; he will inevitably be arrogant, he will be proud. Therefore in the Bible having the identity of the poor man is not so much a matter of being materially poor, but of the fact that this existential situation of life has led him not to rebel against life, as often happens in the face of pain and negative things. This existential situation has led him rather to mature a great wisdom of life, to acquire that heart full of wisdom of which the Psalms also speak: «Teach us to number our days that we may gain a heart of wisdom» (Ps 90:12). Therefore the poor man in this sense becomes, as an effect of his situation, humble, modest, gentle, yielding, but not because he has a submissive spirit, rather because he has acquired true wisdom, has discovered God in the poverty of things, has reached the richness of possessing God; whereas the rich man, by his very situation, is led to become proud, arrogant, because he has never had the experience of someone placing himself before him to make him feel his limits. So the poor man who has succeeded in this sense becomes honest, respects others, because he has learned from life, whereas the rich man becomes wicked, because he makes himself his own law. And this can also concern our small religious world, our personal world, when we want to make our own things absolute and try to maneuver and manage our own living spaces, whereby we too become arrogant and wicked…

Saturday

TC pp. 366-368, «It is I who guide… return to your stocks»

«It is I who guide your steps» - My Good: your words are unchangeable!

My voice:

- Leave her to the direction of the field and go elsewhere: there you will find a good and zealous shepherd who will hand over his flock to you.

I set out, and as I went I kept repeating to myself: where could he be? why, dear voice, do you not tell me where this shepherd is to be found? you are so kind as to teach me, and yet you send me groping like this? How much pain I feel from the fear of going wrong! My voice:

- This cannot be, because it is I who guide your steps!

At this answer I prostrated myself on the ground and, with arms outstretched in the sign of the cross, I gave thanks to the Most High. I began to recite the prayer of the most holy Virgin and, swifter than ever, I quickened my pace. Arrived at the foot of a cliff, there was no longer any way to go on. I would have climbed if I could have scrambled up, but I had to stop without moving. I did not complain nor think about where I was: nothing! I sat down and, quite joyful, (I said):

- My Good, your words are unchangeable!

I was full of faith that my God could also in an instant turn that mountain into a royal and delightful plain. Night comes; the torrent that divides the road from the mountain swells: and nothing! I begin to feel a turmoil.

Ever steadfast, I took a few stones and made of them, as best I could, a seat. It grew darker and darker. With my Crucified pressed to my breast, I fell peacefully asleep.

A loud roar woke me. They were black figures, which precisely because of their blackness I could see, though it was deep night without a moon; but in the light of the clear sky objects could be made out fairly well. One of those shadows, the tallest, came close to me and told me to go with him, that he would lead me to a charming farmhouse where there were kind people waiting for me.

- Who are you? - I said to him calmly.

- I am a man of that house who learned that you are here alone and, out of the charity of those people, I was sent here.

- Liar! go away!

- No! - he answered me - You are deceived. The voice that told you it was with you is I; I will give you proofs: if you do not come with me I will show you the truth!

I answered him in a severe tone:

- Buffoon! go away! for in the name of my God I will show you what faith can do.

He began to sneer, mocking me:

- Faith! - he repeated to me - Split this mountain, then!

- I will certainly do it! - I said to him. And he:

- Before you can do that, I with all my followers will undo you and carry you off with us.

- I tell you - I said to him - to withdraw!

Meanwhile, I hear that a troop of others is arriving. I rose and said to him:

- Now you will see!

I commanded the mountain to level a road for me to climb, in the name of God. And behold, the road appears, great and beautiful, from the bottom to the summit. They, frightened, looked at me; turning to them, I said: - All of you who wanted to undo me! You may not touch one hair of my head. Return to your stocks.

2nd Sunday of Ordinary Time

D. pp. 49-50, par. 1

As in the Old Testament the Covenant between God and his people was founded on the sacrifice of slaughtered animals and their blood sprinkled on the defiled purified them, so the new Covenant is founded on the blood of Christ. In Him, in fact, who through an eternal spirit offered himself without blemish to God, our conscience is cleansed from dead works, to serve him in holiness and justice (cf. Heb 9:14).

Of this mystery of the economy of salvation Rosa lives the mystical experience. She sees several times in vision the ransom of her sins:

«…For a long time… he showed me two books… In them were written certain names and then Saints; at the end was my name written large and then Saint; written prominently in the other, which was large, were my sins, more than half of it was written and I saw them all canceled with the Blood of my Dear Redeemer…» (M. 1.1, p. 5).

The «precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish or spot» (1 Pt

1:18f), is a symbol of redemption (cf. Mt 26:28). The beginning of Rosa's conversion is marked by this symbolic presence of the Blood of Christ. She is purified by the blood to deserve to be among those who «have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb, are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple» (Rev 7:14f).

Her life passes through the experience of the shedding of blood and remains as a precious witness to the incommensurable value of the «blood» of Christ in the redemptive action.

Monday

D. pp. 81-82, «The promise of Jesus is fulfilled… that she must live in love»

These ineffable moments nourish an ever higher perception of the Presence that Jesus promised to the soul that loves him.

Rosa is one of these souls who, loving him, deserves the fulfillment of Jesus' promise:

«Oh! my Love, what you make me experience in this your Heart. Oh! if man could come to understand what greatness is experienced in this Love, surely he would not hesitate a minute to cast away those affections that soon wither. Only your Love increases every day and, better said, never ends» (M. 1.1, p. 46).

She discovers that the secret to having her Good present is to associate herself with his redemptive mystery; for this reason she arrives at the full acceptance of suffering:

«While I was in the fierce persecutions, behold my God comes to comfort me. What could I do but wish that others would come soon, because that way my Good came to comfort me? Oh! your caresses!…»

«Tribulations, sorrows rained upon me from every side. But how to feel them, nothing! In my love everything is absorbed by the sweetness of his Love. Yes, strike, for this donkey is hard and my soul rejoices greatly. An indescribable calm. Last night as I was about to take my rest as usual upon the cross I felt myself rapt» (M. 1.1, p. 117; 157).

By her dedication she can feel addressed to herself the words of God: «I will betroth you to me in faithfulness» (Hos 2:22). Her faith becomes, in fact, ever more fidelity, adherence to the will of God. This adherence is all the more solid in that, within the soul, her Good bears witness to his presence by a light that is a participation in the divine light. Rosa therefore walks the path of sanctification willed by Him, following the light.

Out of love she unites herself to her most holy God, and for this very reason she is bound to sanctify herself, but since God is love, she understands that she must live in love.

Tuesday

FS pp. 145-146, «If the love of God… every consolation: everything in a word!»

If the love of God was the subject that most set her aflame when she spoke to the sisters, fraternal charity was the most frequent, indeed one may say it was the fulcrum of her pedagogy. And these were not fine reflections on the queen of virtues: Mother Rosa wanted mutual love to show itself in the concrete attitudes of daily life, in mutual attentions, in solicitous collaboration, in knowing how to overcome selfishness, misunderstandings, grumbling and the other enemies of fraternal living. Superiors especially had to be models and builders of such unity.

See the three conferences on fraternal charity given in April 1890, those addressed to the voting members of the general chapter on the theme Will and Love in 1895, and those addressed to the superiors of Sicily in April 1898 (M 10.2, pp. 1-6; 10.5; 10.6).

In those conferences and in her letters she insistently urges superiors: an equal manner with all the sisters, without discrimination or preference, without humiliating those who come from a family of lower standing; understanding of personal conditions and situations; gentleness and sweetness in correcting. Above all it is the superior's task to create in her community a healthy and joyful climate of true fraternal charity. A few of her many beautiful recommendations will suffice:

«Ah dear superior! I assure you that merely writing these two lines that speak of charity I feel in myself a strong desire, and for what? My God, calm, calm this in me, because it makes me suffer too much… When this thought seizes my mind, I do not know how to contain it»

- «Pray and love one another all with the same love, and take care to reach that beautiful unity of thinking, of acting; tend toward a center, which is God»

- «True charity and love toward you must be so sincere that one's own good must also be the sister's. If you become so, the Spirit of God will reign in you for an eternity» - «Love one another, and let charity be what accompanies you in all your actions»

- «When I speak of charity, it seems I would never stop; I find everything in it, every consolation: everything in a word!» (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 1867, 3/9/1870, 3/25/1872; to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, 2/4/1871).

Wednesday

FS pp. 140-141, «The love of God was her theme… impression on the Sisters»

The love of God was her favorite theme when she spoke to the sisters and it was also the one they most gladly heard from her lips; in her the Gospel saying was fulfilled: Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Mt 12:34). Her words - the sisters themselves testify - came forth aflame and penetrated hearts, kindling them with the love of God (Summ., p. 63, 872). The text of the conference given on March 14, 1872 to the community of Sampierdarena has been preserved, faithfully transcribed by the secretary Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino. It begins by stating: «Human tongue is not good enough to explain what the love of God is». The philosophers, the moralists, the ascetics «will know nothing of how to define it». One must turn to the saints who experienced it: Catherine of Genoa, Catherine of Siena, Teresa of Jesus, Francis of Assisi,

Philip Neri «Neither science nor the mind of man is needed to understand what this love is, which can be had from God alone, and which no one is able to describe unless he has tasted it».

Then, leaving aside the examples of the saints, great lovers, she opens her interior with sincerity, though speaking in the third person, to describe how she experiences the love of God and the fires of love. To the objection, which she guesses in her listeners, that it is a free gift of God, she replies that three dispositions are needed to receive it: prayer, stripping oneself of one's own will, and the longing to suffer. Even today one feels the emotion of that unprepared outpouring vibrate in every word, which must have made a strong impression on the sisters.

Thursday

D. pp. 131-133, par. 5

The experiences of the pre-paschal Christ must mark Rosa's life so that she may build up the portion of the people entrusted to her, and in this and with this the Church.

Jesus is at root the holy Remnant, the Servant, the Son, the temple, the firstborn of the new people; the «God with us», the kingdom that is already coming, set in our midst.

In a first stage, therefore, the Church lives conversion to him, sets out to follow him, accepts the constitutive elements of his Covenant, becomes Jesus himself who takes upon himself the sins and responsibilities of humanity. (14).

Rosa is wholly involved by God in the dynamism of being immersed in the historical events of the Church and in her mystical sorrow:

«The thought of what the Church was suffering was most painful to me and at times I fainted, so strong was the pain. The Head of the Church imprisoned, Pius the Ninth, my father! Oh, what anguish!… I always feel myself failing, I am in agony, what will it be, my Good, do you leave me so, do you say nothing to me?…».

«…I saw the Holy Mother veiled (I saw the picture covered with a veil). Oh, what pain I did not feel for two days!… at the end of the two days I saw her as usual without a veil. I begged her so much to tell me something. A sorrowful voice said to me: Rome, the great tribulations» (M. 1.2, pp. 29; 31).

The initiative of taking part intensely in the mystery of the Church is many times God's, so that she is not immediately given to see and understand what she lives: «I am in the greatest desolation: horrible temptations against the Church. And who? My God, I am a monster of infamy! while for the Pope and the Princes Cardinals, the Bishops, what would I not do?

My life is nothing to offer for the prosperity of the Church. Alas! how painful this state is to me!» (M. 5.2, p. 46).

She experiences, therefore, in herself the echo of the sins of others and the torment of fearing that it is she herself who wants and cultivates certain feelings against the Church. And she is also called to share mystically in the passion of the mystical Body of Christ.

Jesus himself enlightens her, as she herself writes, on the meaning and value of her experiences in the Church:

«What I have suffered, my God! First something came to me that I cannot describe and I said: «O my Love! what is this that I feel?» - They are the sufferings that the Church endures» (M. 5.3, p. 74f).

She can say with Paul: «none of us lives for himself and none of us dies for himself» (Rom 14:7). «If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it» (1 Cor 12:26-27). «Love does not insist on its own way» (1 Cor 13:5).

Friday

Pr.Po. pp. 47-50, par. 1

Prayers concerning his mission

A first text presents us with Jesus who «went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor» (Lk 6:12-16). This mention of prayer in Luke tells us that He prays before choosing the twelve, because it is a decisive moment of his messianic activity, since Jesus, with the choice of the Twelve, is laying the foundations of the new people of God; this is why he chooses twelve: they must constitute a historical replica of the twelve Patriarchs of the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus, with his messianic activity, inaugurates the new «people of God», that of the «last times». Yet it is not a radically new people, having nothing to do with the preceding one. In himself, Jesus came for Israel: «I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel» (Mt 15:24). Obviously the promises of God can never fail, and therefore the radius has widened with the opening to all who will believe, but without excluding from the new people of God the historical Israel, which in fact had excluded itself by its refusal.

The Twelve, therefore, are the twelve new Patriarchs of the new universal people of God.

For this reason, after Easter we see the concern to restore the group, now lacking a member with the departure of Judas. Peter then takes the floor and declares this necessity in programmatic fashion (Acts 1:21-22). Here too they first pray and the choice is left to God; they cast lots and let God choose.
